title: 17,500-ton nuclear submarine surfaces after record 217 days underwater
content: Seven months without sunlight, fresh air, or the ability to reply to a single message from home — that’s the life of sailors living in submarines. For the 140 sailors aboard 15,900-tonne (17,526-ton) HMS Vengeance, that reality finally ended recently when the Royal Navy submarine surfaced and sailed back to its Scottish base at Faslane.Carrying Trident nuclear missiles, the vessel completed a record-breaking 217 days submerged beneath the ocean surface. This is said to be the longest continuous undersea deployment in British naval history. Reportedly, it breaks the previous 205-day record set by sister ship HMS Vanguard just months ago in April.Harsh conditions at seaBBC reported that the Defense Secretary, Wes Streeting, stood at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome the crew home. As the 492-foot submarine glided up Gare Loch flanked by tugboats, its hull told the story of its prolonged isolation. Thick marine growth covered the exterior, and several of its specialized sound-absorbing tiles had been stripped away during the seven-month mission.Life inside the Vanguard-class submarine operates under extreme secrecy to maintain the United Kingdom’s continuous nuclear deterrent. Since 1969, Britain has kept at least one ballistic missile submarine hidden at sea to ensure a retaliatory strike capability in the event of a nuclear attack. To avoid enemy detection, HMS Vengeance remained in strict radio silence after departing on April 12.Sailors worked six-hour shifts and slept in cramped bunks, up to nine per cabin. Their sole connection to loved ones was the weekly “Familygram,” a heavily vetted 120-word note sent from home. Sailors are strictly forbidden from replying, and officials even withhold bad news if it threatens to compromise a crew member’s focus.Fleet maintenance issuesReturning to dry land brings its own disorienting challenges. After breathing nothing but recycled, filtered air for over half a year, sailors often find the natural smells of the outside world completely overwhelming. Living in cramped metal corridors also warps their depth perception, prompting naval doctors to ban the crew from driving for several days while their eyes and brains readjust to open horizons.The record-breaking mission highlights a growing strain on the Royal Navy’s aging submarine fleet. Patrols usually lasted around three months, but six-month deployments have become the exhausting new normal.HMS Vengeance was actually scheduled to return last weekend, though a last-minute technical fault forced its replacement vessel back to port for repairs. The broader fleet faces similar challenges. Commissioned in the 1990s with a 25-year lifespan, the four Vanguard-class boats are being pushed to serve for up to 40 years until the new Dreadnought-class submarines arrive in the early 2030s.Currently, HMS Victorious is tied up in a £560 million deep maintenance overhaul that began in 2023, leaving only three boats operational to carry the entire burden of Britain’s nuclear defense. A four-year delay in starting the Dreadnought replacement submarine program, combined with a slow 15-year construction timeline, has created severe operational and financial consequences.According to a recent Treasury study, delaying the project to save money in the short term has forced costly life extensions for the aging Vanguard submarines and increased operational risks. Addressing concerns over the resulting lengthy patrols, the First Sea Lord emphasized that maintaining the nation’s nuclear deterrent is his top priority, making improvements to submarine maintenance and readiness his primary daily focus.

title: US: Robots play piano, mimic human eye gaze with artificial muscles
content: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed artificial muscles that give soft robots more precise control over their movements. Inspired by small muscles in human hands and eyes, the technology can produce controlled movements, hold intermediate positions, and coordinate with other artificial muscles. The muscles combine liquid crystal elastomers, graphene, and an embedded copper coil to convert electrical signals into muscle-like motion.Demonstrations include a robotic finger pressing individual piano keys and artificial eyes shifting their gaze through controlled movements, highlighting the technology’s potential for fine motor skills in soft robotics.Robots gain muscleArtificial muscles let soft robots perform precise movements by combining flexible materials with built-in sensing and feedback control.The technology, called CoilLCE, draws inspiration from the small muscles responsible for delicate movements in human fingers and eyes. It combines liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs), graphene, and an ultrathin embedded copper coil to create artificial muscle fibers that convert electrical signals into controlled mechanical motion.The team developed the artificial muscles to address a limitation in conventional soft robotic actuators. While traditional robotic motors can provide precise movement, they often require bulky components and complex mechanical arrangements that make it difficult to replicate the flexibility and compactness of biological muscles.The researchers drew inspiration from the small muscles in human fingers and eyes to design the systems.LCEs offer a potential alternative because they change shape when heated. However, controlling their movement presents a challenge. As the material heats up, it contracts, while cooling causes it to return toward its original shape. This makes it difficult to maintain a specific intermediate position without continuous monitoring and adjustment.“This is the first time that feedback control has been demonstrated on an LCE actuator and it is a necessary step for these sorts of artificial muscles to be able to be used in future robotic applications,” said Cynthia Sung, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM) at Penn Engineering, in a statement.Precision muscle controlTo improve their performance, the researchers combined LCEs with graphene. The graphene makes the resulting material softer and tougher, allowing it to stretch while withstanding the mechanical forces generated when artificial muscles work against one another.The researchers then embedded an ultrathin copper coil inside the LCE-graphene fibers. The coil performs two functions: it generates heat to activate the artificial muscle and acts as a sensor by measuring changes in electrical resistance as the material moves.These resistance measurements provide feedback about the muscle’s state, allowing the control system to adjust heating power in real time. By keeping the electrical resistance near a predetermined target, the system can regulate contraction and maintain intermediate positions for extended periods.This closed-loop approach eliminates the need for a separate position sensor, reducing the number of components required to control the artificial muscles. The researchers also demonstrated feedback control with an LCE actuator, addressing an important challenge in making these materials suitable for practical robotic applications.The team demonstrated the technology using an artificial hand and a pair of robotic eyes. In the hand, artificial fingers pressed individual piano keys, paused, and moved to subsequent notes. The robotic eyes used four pairs of opposing actuators to reproduce controlled gaze movements.The arrangement mimics biological muscles, where opposing muscle groups work together to move. When one artificial muscle contracts, its counterpart stretches, allowing the system to control movement without actively driving every muscle at once. This configuration can also reduce the number of control inputs needed.The researchers see potential applications in humanoid robots, particularly artificial faces that require numerous small actuators working together to reproduce natural expressions. However, integrating larger numbers of artificial muscles into coordinated systems remains a challenge. The team plans to explore AI and computer vision to manage more complex movements and interactions.

title: Mystery of universe's evolution to be decoded with Evolve+ spacecraft bus
content: NASA has selected BAE Systems to support PRIMA astrophysics program. BAE Systems will provide its Evolve+ spacecraft bus for the mission. It will also help to lead the observatory assembly, integration and test process, and serve as the operations and ground lead for NASA’s JPL, the manager of the mission. NASA to make significant discoveries“We are excited to continue our decades-long partnership with JPL through the PRIMA mission that will enable NASA to make significant discoveries on the history of the universe,” said Bonnie Patterson, vice president and general manager of civil space for BAE Systems. “The PRIMA mission will also help fill observation gaps with other NASA astrophysics missions, including the James Webb Space Telescope and other observatories, also supported by BAE Systems.”NASA’s PRIMA mission will use a highly sensitive, far-infrared space telescope that is designed to see parts of the universe that are hidden by dust. Using a 1.8-meter diameter telescope, it will observe the cosmos in far-infrared light, bridging the critical observation gap between the James Webb Space Telescope and ground-based radio observatories, according to a press release. Mission will help scientists learn how stars, planets, and galaxiesThe mission will help scientists learn how stars, planets, galaxies and even water formed over time. It will reveal how these cosmic structures grow and change, providing a clearer picture of how our universe developed and evolved from its formation to the present.The company will provide its Evolve+ spacecraft bus, a key platform that supports the spacecraft’s essential systems and enables the telescope to operate in space. It will also lead the observatory’s assembly, integration and testing activities, ensuring that the spacecraft and its scientific instruments are brought together and prepared for the demanding conditions of space.The PRIMA mission is currently advancing through Phase B development and is targeted for launch in 2033 for a five-year mission. Following a NASA confirmation review, the project will move toward full implementation.At the heart of the PRIMA mission is a highly sensitive far-infrared space telescope designed to observe cosmic objects and phenomena that remain hidden from conventional optical telescopes.Many important astronomical processes take place within dense clouds of dust and gas. These cosmic environments often obscure visible light, making it difficult for scientists to study the formation of stars, planets and galaxies. Far-infrared observations offer a way to penetrate these dusty regions and reveal processes that would otherwise remain largely inaccessible.The PRIMA programme represents more than a new aerospace contract. It highlights the growing importance of advanced spacecraft platforms, precision engineering and integrated mission operations in enabling ambitious scientific exploration.As NASA continues to expand its astrophysics programme, missions such as PRIMA will play an important role in addressing unanswered questions about the origins and evolution of the universe.With its far-infrared observation capabilities, international industrial collaboration and support from experienced space technology providers, PRIMA has the potential to open a new window into the cosmos.The programme further strengthens its position as a key technology partner in NASA’s scientific exploration efforts. For the wider scientific community, it represents another promising step towards understanding the complex processes that shaped the universe and continue to influence its evolution today.

title: US' 9,300-ton warship gets new communication that works in extreme condition
content: One of the powerful destroyers of the U.S. Navy has got a new type of communication system. L3Harris Technologies has successfully completed U.S. Navy operational testing of its FleetLink communications system aboard an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer. The testing demonstrated the system’s ability to support maritime interoperability and reliable communications under operational conditions. “Interoperability is a foundational requirement for the Navy’s increasingly complex operations,” said Faisal Munir, President, Mission Critical Communications, Communications & Spectrum Dominance, L3Harris. “FleetLink demonstrates exactly how the equipment will perform under real-world conditions to ensure combat readiness and provide commanders with seamless surface and undersea communications.”Modernizing naval communication infrastructureThe successful testing marks an important step in advancing the U.S. Navy’s efforts to modernize its naval communications infrastructure and strengthen connectivity across increasingly complex maritime operations.FleetLink is a high-speed, modular communications solution developed by L3Harris to bring together multiple radios and waveforms into an integrated system. Designed to replace legacy communications equipment, the system enables rapid integration of data from multiple sources while enhancing secure information exchange between naval platforms, according to a press release.A key feature of FleetLink is its latest National Security Agency (NSA)-certified cryptographic capability, which is intended to support secure and resilient communications. The system is designed to help naval forces maintain reliable connectivity and information sharing in demanding operational environments.Increasingly important requirement for modern naval forcesInteroperability has become an increasingly important requirement for modern naval forces, particularly as maritime operations involve multiple platforms, communication networks and operational domains.The successful completion of FleetLink’s operational testing highlights the growing importance of advanced communications technologies in modern maritime operations. As naval forces face increasingly complex operational environments, secure, reliable and interoperable communications are essential for maintaining situational awareness, coordinating activities and supporting timely command decisions.By integrating multiple radios and waveforms into a modular architecture, FleetLink seeks to address the limitations associated with legacy communications systems while providing a more flexible approach to naval connectivity. L3Harris developed the FleetLink system under the Navy’s Scalable, Modular, Radio Cluster contract in 2023. The system includes three configurations, including four-channel high-frequency, four-channel multi-band and submarine multi-band variants, as per the release.With its modular architecture, multiple system configurations and NSA-certified cryptographic capability, FleetLink is designed to support secure information exchange and reliable connectivity across surface and undersea naval platforms.As the U.S. Navy continues to modernise its communications infrastructure, technologies such as FleetLink are expected to play an important role in supporting operational readiness and the evolving requirements of modern naval warfare. The new communications system aims to strengthen secure information exchange, operational readiness and connectivity across surface and undersea naval platforms.The successful operational testing of FleetLink aboard an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer represents a significant milestone in L3Harris’ efforts to advance maritime communications interoperability.

title: China’s HQ-17A offers missile protection for troops near Taiwan Strait
content: China’s mobile HQ-17A air-defense system could play an important role in protecting amphibious forces and military equipment assembled along the mainland coast ahead of a potential operation against Taiwan. A recent exercise showed a wheeled launcher engaging a drone simulating an incoming cruise missile while amphibious armored vehicles moved toward open water, highlighting how the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) could provide short-range air cover for troops preparing to cross the Taiwan Strait.The system is designed to move alongside ground formations and engage aircraft, cruise missiles and precision-guided weapons. Its wheeled configuration also allows it to launch missiles while moving, potentially keeping armored columns protected without requiring them to stop and wait for air-defense coverage.HQ-17A provides mobile air cover for amphibious formationsThe exercise that happened last June involved amphibious armored vehicles moving into open water while a six-wheeled HQ-17A launcher positioned along the coastline fired at a drone simulating an incoming cruise missile. The unit involved was believed to belong to the PLA’s 125th Amphibious Combined Arms Brigade. A US Army analysis identified the formation as one of six amphibious brigades considered central to a potential landing operation against Taiwan, the South China Morning Post reported.Each launcher carries eight vertically launched missiles and an onboard radar, allowing it to detect and engage aerial targets independently. The missiles have an engagement range of approximately 0.9 to 9.3 miles and can intercept targets flying between roughly 33 feet and 32,808 feet above the ground.A typical battery consists of four launchers supported by command and ammunition vehicles. The tracked HQ-17 can search for targets while moving but must stop to fire, whereas the HQ-17A is reported to engage up to four targets simultaneously and launch missiles while travelling at speeds of up to 15.5 mph.Eight missiles and radar dependence create vulnerabilitiesDespite its mobility, the HQ-17A has limitations that could become significant during a prolonged conflict involving large numbers of drones and precision-guided weapons. Each launcher carries eight ready-to-fire missiles, half the 16 reportedly carried by newer Russian Tor-M2 launchers. Reloading an HQ-17 or HQ-17A takes approximately 18 minutes, potentially creating a vulnerable period during which a launcher has reduced engagement capacity. Its radar-based guidance also creates opportunities for adversaries to detect and target the system. Operating close to the coastline, where Taiwanese drones, rockets and missiles could threaten military staging areas, would require crews to maintain situational awareness and coordinate with other air-defense units.Furthermore, Taiwan is expanding its own uncrewed capabilities. In August, its legislature approved a six-year, approximately $7.3 billion, funding framework covering uncrewed systems, including coastal attack and reconnaissance drones, SCMP adds.The PLA is also exploring ways to protect amphibious troops after they leave the coastline. During the June exercise, soldiers aboard amphibious vehicles fired shoulder-launched missiles at drones. However, even a coordinated network would not guarantee complete protection, and its effectiveness would depend on overlapping radar coverage, communication between units, ammunition availability and the ability to detect threats early enough to engage them.

title: US’ top nuclear rival upgrades Mach-6 ballistic missile for accuracy
content: Russia has added optical and radar-homing upgrades to its Iskander ballistic missiles in a bid to improve their accuracy along the Dnipro River in Ukraine. The improved accuracy aims to sever logistical ties between the left and right banks of the river and degrade living conditions in Ukrainian cities ahead of the upcoming winter. Since early October, Russia has stepped up attacks on key bridges and power grids in Ukraine in a bid to bring down infrastructure and logistical support available in key cities. On October 1-2, Russia attacked the South Bridge in Kyiv, while targeting the North Bridge on October 3-4. The Central Bridge in Dnipro city was struck on October 30, while the cable-stayed bridge in Zaporizhzhia was made a target on Oct. 6. The North Bridge was attacked again last week. But with a difference. While the previous attacks consisted of jet-powered drones, the attack last weekend consisted of Iskander ballistic missiles with upgraded homing heads. Why use ballistic missiles? Since the beginning of the conflict, Ukraine has deployed smarter electronic warfare (EW) to counter Russian aggression where possible. This layer of defense jams the electronics of incoming projectiles and minimizes the damage caused. While bridges are narrow structural targets, the drone attacks could not achieve the desired results, forcing Russia to change its strategy. Ballistic missiles are rocket-propelled weapons with a wide range spectrum and can carry a range of powerful warheads. The Iskander is a short-range ballistic missile with a range of 310 miles (500 km) and can carry high-explosive fragmentation, fuel-air explosives, and even thermonuclear warheads. Irrespective of the range or warhead, ballistic missiles work on the same principle: they take powered flight to gain speed and altitude. The engine then shuts off, and the missile follows a parabolic arc and heads toward the target at high velocity. When the missile reaches its desired altitude, the onboard computer positions it in the line of its target. However, the path is guided by gravity and comes with a wide margin for error. This makes the missiles unsuitable for precise targets like bridges. But Russia’s upgrade changes that completely. Russia’s upgraded missilesRussian upgrade of the Iskander ballistic missiles features radar and optical homing seekers. These enable the missiles to alter flight trajectories in the terminal phase of their flight, increasing accuracy to a few meters. The aim is to hit the bridges more accurately, as was seen through four Iskander missile strikes on the North Bridge in Kyiv last weekend. Ukrainian authorities expect these attacks to intensify as they head into the winter. According to Ukrainian media reports, Russian strategy is to target key bridges along the Dnipro River to paralyze both military and civilian logistics on both the banks. Military strategy and technology experts have confirmed that Russian upgrades have likely increased the accuracy of the missiles. However, their ability to bring down Kyiv’s key bridges is also dependent on the quality of engineering of Ukraine’s bridges. Key river crossings in Ukraine are heavily engineered and for now the likelihood of Russia being able to destroy them remains fairly low.

title: 7 weapons that have changed the scale of destruction in modern warfare
content: In an ideal world, there would be no wars, and humanity would have little reason to develop weapons designed to destroy lives on such an enormous scale. Unfortunately, conflict has been a recurring part of human history, driving the development of increasingly destructive technologies.From nuclear bombs capable of devastating entire cities to chemical agents and explosives that can threaten civilians long after fighting ends, some weapons have consequences that extend far beyond the battlefield. Their impact is measured not just in immediate casualties, but also in lasting environmental damage, displacement, illness, and generations of human suffering.There is no universally accepted ranking of the world’s deadliest weapons. But these seven stand out for their destructive potential and the devastating consequences they can have when used.1. Nuclear weaponsFew weapons come close to the destructive power of a nuclear bomb. A single detonation can produce an enormous blast, intense heat, and dangerous radiation, destroying buildings and overwhelming emergency services. The consequences can persist for generations.The most powerful nuclear device ever detonated was the Soviet Union’s Tsar Bomba, tested over Novaya Zemlya on October 30, 1961. Its estimated yield was 50 megatons of TNT, around 3,300 times the explosive yield of the Hiroshima bomb.That was a test device, not an operational weapon. But the threat today comes from the thousands of nuclear warheads held by countries around the world. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimated that nine nuclear-armed states possessed approximately 12,241 warheads at the beginning of 2025.2. Intercontinental ballistic missilesAn intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) is a delivery system rather than a warhead, but it makes nuclear weapons particularly dangerous by allowing them to travel across continents.ICBMs can carry nuclear warheads over thousands of miles, with some designed to release multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). These allow one missile to carry several warheads aimed at different targets.The combination of long range, high speed, and multiple warheads makes strategic missile systems among the most consequential weapons ever developed. Their existence also creates the risk of rapid escalation during a crisis, particularly when warning times are short.3. Biological weaponsBiological weapons turn microorganisms or toxins into instruments of warfare. They can involve bacteria, viruses, or substances produced by living organisms, deliberately released to cause disease or death.Anthrax, plague, and botulinum toxin are among the biological agents of serious public-health concern. Some biological threats are particularly difficult to contain because an infectious disease can spread beyond the initial exposure and potentially trigger an epidemic.Unlike a conventional explosion, a biological attack may not be immediately recognizable. Its effects could emerge over time, placing enormous pressure on healthcare systems and public-health authorities.The Biological Weapons Convention, which entered into force in 1975, prohibits the development, production, acquisition, transfer, stockpiling, and use of biological and toxin weapons.4. Chemical nerve agentsChemical weapons use toxic substances to injure or kill. Among the most dangerous are nerve agents such as sarin and VX, which interfere with the nervous system’s ability to regulate vital bodily functions.These substances can cause severe symptoms, including seizures, paralysis, and respiratory failure. VX is particularly concerning because it can remain dangerous on surfaces for extended periods, depending on environmental conditions.Chemical weapons have been used in modern conflicts, including the Iran-Iraq War and the Syrian civil war. Their effects can extend beyond immediate casualties, leaving survivors with lasting health problems and communities struggling with contamination.The Chemical Weapons Convention prohibits the development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons.5. Thermobaric weaponsOften called fuel-air or vacuum bombs, thermobaric weapons are designed to produce intense heat and prolonged blast pressure. They use oxygen from the surrounding air as part of their explosive process, creating a powerful pressure wave.Their effects can be particularly destructive in enclosed spaces such as tunnels, bunkers, and buildings, where blast waves can reflect off surrounding surfaces. The resulting injuries can include severe burns, internal trauma, and respiratory damage.Russia’s TOS-1A heavy flamethrower system is one well-known platform associated with thermobaric ammunition. Despite the nickname, these systems are not conventional flamethrowers; they launch rockets carrying specialized warheads.6. The GBU-43/B MOABThe US military’s GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, better known as the Mother of All Bombs, is among the largest conventional bombs ever developed.Weighing approximately 21,000 pounds (9,525 kg), the GPS-guided weapon is designed to produce a massive blast overpressure against large-area targets and structures such as tunnels and cave complexes.The MOAB was used in combat for the first time on April 13, 2017, when the United States dropped it on an ISIS-occupied cave complex in Afghanistan.Despite its enormous size, it is not a nuclear weapon. Its destructive power is considerably smaller than even a relatively low-yield nuclear device, but it remains one of the most powerful conventional weapons in the US arsenal.7. Cluster munitionsCluster munitions are designed to scatter numerous smaller explosive devices, known as submunitions, across a wide area. They can be delivered by aircraft, rockets, or artillery systems.Their danger does not end when the initial attack is over. Some submunitions fail to explode on impact, effectively turning fields, roads, and residential areas into minefields that can remain dangerous for years.Children and civilians returning to damaged communities are particularly vulnerable to unexploded devices. According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, at least 1,063 people were killed or injured by cluster munitions in 2025, with civilians accounting for 87% of recorded casualties.The 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions prohibits their use, production, stockpiling, and transfer for states that are party to it.The destructive legacy of modern warfareThe true cost of these weapons cannot be measured by their explosive power or technological sophistication alone. Nuclear weapons can threaten entire populations, biological and chemical agents can leave lasting health consequences, and unexploded munitions can continue claiming civilian lives long after a war has ended.Ideally, technological progress would be directed toward improving lives rather than finding new ways to destroy them. Until then, understanding the destructive potential of these weapons is also a reminder of why preventing their use, limiting their proliferation, and protecting civilians must remain priorities.

title: 7 cargo aircraft being developed to fly without pilots
content: Several companies and militaries are testing uncrewed cargo aircraft that can haul supplies without a pilot onboard. From hybrid-electric cargo aircraft to heavy-lift fixed-wing planes, these planes are moving from concept toward real-world operations. They are already being used to deliver medical supplies, packages, and military cargo in remote areas. Some have already completed uncrewed flight demonstrations, while others are still in development. Let us look at the seven groundbreaking models leading the transformation.1. Elroy Air ChaparralHybrid-electric cargo aircraft designed for autonomous vertical takeoff and landingThe US-based Elroy Air’s Chaparral is among the most advanced projects in this category. The hybrid-electric aircraft uses vertical-lift propellers to take off and land without a runway, while a separate propulsion system supports forward flight.It is designed to carry more than 500 pounds (227 kg) of cargo over distances of up to 450 miles (724 km). Its modular cargo pods can transport medical supplies, spare parts, and other deliveries without requiring ground infrastructure at the destination.In September 2026, Chaparral completed a series of autonomous, uncrewed cargo flights in Louisiana under the Federal Aviation Administration’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The aircraft transported packages, medical supplies, tools, food, and water under air traffic control oversight, without a pilot on board. The demonstration brings the project closer to commercial operations.2. Skyways SkyreachLong-range hybrid-powered autonomous VTOL aircraftSkyways unveiled its Skyreach autonomous cargo aircraft in November 2026, with customer flights scheduled to begin in December. Developed from the company’s V3 Block 2 platform, it combines eight electric motors for vertical takeoff and landing with fuel-powered propulsion for forward flight.The aircraft is designed for more than 18 hours of flight and an operational range exceeding 1,300 miles (2,092 km) under its maximum-fuel configuration. Its seven-cubic-foot (0.2 cubic meters) cargo bay can accommodate different payloads, including temperature-controlled cargo.Skyreach has a combined fuel-and-payload capacity of 100 pounds (45 kg), so its maximum range depends on how much cargo it carries. The project is backed by a $37 million US Air Force AFWERX STRATFI award intended to support full-rate production. Skyways says production has started in Austin, Texas, following the completion of its production design and progress in flight qualification testing.3. Poseidon Aerospace EgretLarge uncrewed fixed-wing cargo aircraftPoseidon Aerospace is developing Egret as a larger alternative to small cargo drones. The aircraft has a planned wingspan of approximately 50 feet ( about 15 meters) and is designed to transport up to 4,000 pounds (1,814 kg) of cargo over more than 1,000 nautical miles (1,151 miles).Unlike vertical-takeoff aircraft, Egret uses conventional runways, including paved and unpaved airstrips. Its design includes both front and rear cargo doors to simplify loading and unloading.Poseidon raised $60 million in Series A funding in September 2026 to advance flight testing and establish its first production line. The company expects the full-scale aircraft to conduct its first uncrewed flight by the end of 2026. Its earlier quarter-scale Seagull demonstrator has already flown, helping validate elements of the aircraft’s design and control architecture.Egret is designed for autonomous operation or remote control, rather than carrying a pilot onboard.4. Zuri uncrewed cargo VTOLHybrid-electric tiltrotor designed for offshore and remote deliveriesCzech aerospace company Zuri unveiled its uncrewed cargo VTOL in August 2026. The hybrid-electric tiltrotor is designed to combine the vertical takeoff capability of a helicopter with the efficiency of fixed-wing flight.Its planned useful load is 165 kg (364 pounds), including fuel and cargo. Zuri estimates a design range of 679 km (422 miles), or 569 km (354 miles) with a 30-minute fuel reserve, at a cruising speed of approximately 220 km/h (137 mph).The aircraft is based on Technology Demonstrator 2.0, a full-scale platform undergoing ground testing and systems integration in Prague. Zuri plans to begin flight testing in early 2027, supported by a €6 million (about $6.9 million) first tranche of Series A financing.Unlike some fully autonomous designs, Zuri’s aircraft will be remotely piloted, with automation handling flight tasks under ground-based supervision.5. Bell 505 uncrewed logistics aircraftAutonomous helicopter being developed for US Marine Corps resupplyBell and Near Earth Autonomy are adapting the Bell 505 helicopter into an uncrewed logistics aircraft for the US Marine Corps’ Medium Aerial Resupply Vehicle – Expeditionary Logistics (MARV-EL) Increment 2 program.The project aims to give Marines a mid-weight cargo aircraft capable of delivering supplies to dispersed units in contested environments. Using an existing helicopter platform could provide access to established manufacturing and maintenance infrastructure while allowing the aircraft to operate without an onboard pilot.Bell announced its selection for the program in April 2026. The development team is integrating Near Earth’s Captain autonomy system and modifying the helicopter’s cargo-handling capabilities. The program is intended to produce a prototype that meets or exceeds the Marine Corps’ performance requirements.The aircraft is still in development, but its military backing gives the project a defined customer and operational requirement.6. Reliable Robotics’ autonomous Cessna Grand CaravanConventional cargo airplane adapted for autonomous flightRather than developing an entirely new aircraft, US company Reliable Robotics is working to automate the Cessna 208B Grand Caravan, a widely used single-engine turboprop.The system uses onboard computers, sensors, and automated flight controls to manage operations such as taxiing, takeoff, navigation, and landing. A remote operator can supervise the aircraft from a ground control station, reducing the need for a pilot in the cockpit.In October 2026, Reliable Robotics completed cargo-flight demonstrations at Albuquerque International Sunport as part of the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The trials used a safety pilot onboard, with the aircraft remotely piloted from the company’s California base. They therefore demonstrated automated and remote operations, rather than routine pilotless commercial service.The project is significant because adapting an existing certified aircraft could offer a more direct route toward autonomous cargo operations than developing a completely new airframe.7. Cessna SkyCourier UXAutonomous medium-payload cargo aircraft concept from Textron and MerlinTextron Aviation and autonomy developer Merlin introduced the Cessna SkyCourier UX concept in September 2026. It combines the existing twin-engine SkyCourier aircraft with Merlin’s Pilot autonomous flight software to explore cargo operations without an onboard crew.The proposed aircraft is intended to carry approximately 6,000 pounds (2,722 kg) of cargo, with space for up to three LD3 containers. It could operate from unimproved runways and support deliveries to remote military bases, expeditionary locations, and other destinations where traditional airlift is difficult to arrange.The concept also explores a more fundamental redesign of the aircraft. Removing the cockpit could free additional space for cargo, with a forward-loading arrangement and integrated loading equipment under consideration.However, SkyCourier UX remains a concept undergoing engineering studies and evaluations. Textron and Merlin have not announced a completed autonomous prototype or a production schedule.

title: 3D-printed hoverboard prototype lifts over copper plate with 22V battery
content: Anyone who has watched Back to the Future II, a science-fiction movie that came out in 1989, has been eagerly waiting to ride the hoverboard that Marty McFly rode. But no one knew how long the wait would be before the technology reached the market.Ten years ago, things began to change as multiple attempts were made over the years to develop the technology. While none has yet delivered a commercially viable hoverboard, enthusiasts continue to push the concept further.Recently, Jake Rogers tried his hand at making a palm-sized hoverboard using 3D-printed material, magnets, brushless motors, and a bunch of knick-knacks from his garage.After spending weeks on the project, he built a miniature hoverboard that he describes as a working prototype that floats above a thick copper plate, completely untethered, with no wheels or air cushion.Halbach configuration for magnetsThe final design houses two rotors spinning in opposite directions, electronic speed controllers (ESP2), a converter that drops the voltage for the board, and two batteries inside the 3D-printed soft pink casing made with polymaker filament.To maximize performance, Rogers also custom-printed the rotors to accommodate a ring of twelve N52 neodymium magnets organized in a Halbach configuration. He chose the specific arrangement to ensure that the strong field points downward while the weak field above remains weak.However, he arrived at this untethered, battery-powered version only after multiple rounds of adjustments and testing. During his early trials, he started with a single motor to lift a lightweight frame off the ground. But the setup with multiple exposed wires was wobbly and twisted erratically due to reaction torque.Battery-powered lift offTo counter the twisting, he paired it with a second motor. At first, the device kept flipping, which he overcame after fixing the jumbled-up wiring. Yet another challenge soon emerged: the magnets kept flinging themselves outward due to strong centrifugal force. By lowering the number of magnets from the initial sixteen to twelve per motor, he reduced the outward force by around 40% while maintaining the same speed.With those issues addressed, Rogers carried out one final redesign. He removed the dead batteries added to balance an earlier chassis and placed live 3S battery packs between the motors. As a result, the compact little board could now glide around on the copper on its own. The untethered flight was made possible by using a battery pack that could supply 22.2 volts when powered on. However, Rogers demonstrated that it wasn’t completely steady yet and still required help to stay level.To better understand the lift force generated by the design, Rogers also placed a sensor on the device and used simulations to perform calculations. According to his estimates, a force of around 61 newtons was exerted on a 3.84-gram magnet rotating at 8,000 rpm, while one entire rotor generated a staggering 941 grams-force at 3,000 rpm with a 5 mm gap. However, he refrained from relying on these simulation-based statistics, as they were generated from a device that rattled vigorously while hovering.Despite those limitations, Rogers believes the concept has room to evolve. Moving forward, he said in his YouTube video that he aims to build a full-size ride-on board, HALO-1, that would require a conductive surface to ride on. However, before chasing that vision, he will first try out a pocket-sized fingerboard toy.​

title: Inflow to world’s largest freshwater lake rebounds to 145%
content: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds about 20 percent of the world’s surface freshwater, and it has been drying up due to adverse effects of climate change. However, a new study has shown that this might be changing – and impressively.Lake Baikal is the world’s oldest and largest freshwater lake, holding about one-fifth of Earth’s unfrozen surface freshwater. This UNESCO World Heritage site relies on water flowing into the lake from the Selenga River and leaving through the Angara River. According to the study, this water balance supports agriculture in Mongolia and hydroelectric power generation in regions along the Angara River, affecting water availability for millions of people. However, in the early 20th century, this streamflow saw a critical decline.Recently, researchers found that streamflow began recovering sharply around 2017, reaching 145.2 percent of its long-term average. The recovery coincided with rising lake levels, increased vegetation growth, and changing Arctic climate conditions.The study, published in Geophysical Research Letters, suggests that changes in atmospheric circulation linked to a regional slowdown in Arctic warming may be helping restore water availability in the Lake Baikal basin.Decades of low water flowShijie Wang of Yunnan University and colleagues reconstructed 343 years of streamflow using tree-ring records. Researchers collected 52 tree-ring cores from pine trees near Lake Baikal and combined them with existing records from 12 additional sites.Their reconstruction revealed intermittent declines beginning in the early 20th century, with streamflow falling to about 90 percent of relatively high levels. Approximately half of all extreme low-flow years occurred after 1900.However, the researchers identified a sharp reversal beginning around 2017. Streamflow recovered to 145.2 percent of its long-term average, while observations showed rising lake levels and increased vegetation growth.The researchers identified 2017–2024 as the most pronounced recovery event in the 343-year record, following a severe decline between 1995 and 2016.Arctic climate changes linked to recoveryResearchers examined environmental factors affecting streamflow, including precipitation, temperature, soil moisture, and snowmelt. Their analysis attributed 59.3 percent of streamflow variability to the combined climatic and ecological factors examined.They also identified significant relationships between streamflow and sea surface temperatures and sea ice cover in parts of the North Pacific and Arctic oceans.Lower sea surface temperatures and higher sea ice cover in the Bering, Chukchi, East Siberian and Okhotsk seas were associated with increased streamflow. According to the study, a regional slowdown in Arctic warming and sea ice retreat coincided with the development of an “Arctic Cold Blob.”Researchers suggested these conditions could alter atmospheric circulation and increase moisture transport toward Lake Baikal. However, further climate modeling is needed to test the proposed connection.Will the recovery last?Despite the findings, researchers have not determined whether the recovery will persist.“Determining whether this wet period is a sustained regime shift or a transient phase is essential for assessing its long-term significance,” the authors wrote. They also cautioned that streamflow estimates for 2015–2024 extend beyond the available instrumental calibration period, introducing uncertainty.The researchers concluded that long-term records are essential for understanding changing water availability and developing adaptive water management strategies.“Our findings indicate that projections relying solely on relatively short instrumental data may not fully capture the basin’s hydroclimatic variability, underestimating the system’s inherent capacity for rapid change,” they wrote.

title: Polymer nanospheres cushion flexible perovskite cells against bending without blocking charge flow
content:
Polymer nanospheres cushion flexible perovskite cells against bending without blocking charge flow
Researchers at the Institute of Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed a way to relieve mechanical stress in flexible perovskite solar cells without the electrical penalty that polymer reinforcement usually brings. The team introduced 50 nm carboxyl-functionalized polymethyl methacrylate nanospheres at the buried interface between the Me-4PACz self-assembled monolayer and the FAPbI₃ perovskite in inverted flexible cells, reporting a power conversion efficiency of 26.02% with a fill factor of 0.845.
Flexible perovskite cells stack polycrystalline thin films with different elastic moduli and mismatched thermal expansion coefficients, so they accumulate residual stress as they heat during the day and cool at night. Because the materials are brittle, that repeated stress opens microcracks, which can eventually let the absorber layer delaminate from the transport layers. Adding polymers to the interface toughens it, but most soft materials are electrically insulating, and they tend to aggregate at grain boundaries or form continuous barriers that impede carrier extraction and depress the fill factor.
Rather than forming a continuous layer, the nanospheres self-assemble into what the researchers describe as a discontinuous nano-island network, covering roughly 12% of the interfacial area at the optimal size and leaving the remaining conductive pathways unobstructed. The elastic spheres modulate the local strain field to dissipate mechanical and thermal stress, while the negatively charged carboxyl surfaces generate a localized electrostatic field that repels electrons and accelerates hole extraction, suppressing non-radiative recombination at the interface. “A polymer interlayer is therefore not only a passive mechanical cushion, it can also preserve electrical pathways in these materials thanks to the utilization of suitable functional groups,” said Dong-Mei Li, one of the paper’s corresponding authors.
The devices showed negligible degradation after 5,000 bending cycles at a 6 mm radius and retained 96.3% of their initial efficiency after 200 thermal cycles between −60 and +80°C. Li notes that commercially available nanospheres and solution-based deposition make the approach practical, though large-area processing and module integration still need validation, along with radiation resistance for space applications. Polymer modification of the buried interface has been pursued along other lines, including
ultrathin PMMA interlayers on sputtered NiOx
a carboxylic-acid-terminated PTAA derivative
that coordinates directly with uncoordinated lead ions.

文章报道了9月20日吉林省主要领导与国家能源局局长王宏志在长春举行的工作会见。双方围绕吉林新能源发展与国家能源安全展开交流：吉林省强调深入落实习近平总书记关于东北振兴和吉林工作的重要指示，加快构建现代化产业体系，推进风光规模化开发、氢能及绿色燃料全产业链布局，绿电装机与绿氢绿氨绿醇产业持续壮大；吉林方面提出支持跨省区绿色甲醇专用通道吉林段率先建设等诉求。国家能源局回应表示，将大力支持“吉电入京”项目建设，拓展吉林新能源外送渠道，探索绿色燃料多场景应用，助力就地消纳与能源绿色转型，服务吉林高质量发展和国家能源安全战略。（198字）
9月1日，国家能源局召开新型电网建设工作部署会，系统总结我国电网发展成就，研判“十五五”时期电力需求年均增长约5%、新能源占比提升、高端产业用能升级等新形势，明确新型电网建设是涵盖新架构、新技术、新服务的系统性变革。会议提出四大重点任务：构建主配微协同的电网新架构；加快人工智能+、柔性构网、智能调控、长时储能等技术攻关与应用；升级新能源并网消纳、高品质供电、算电协同等新服务；守牢大电网安全稳定运行底线。会议强调新型电网建设投资带动效应强，要求加快重大输电通道核准建设，压实地方责任，强化跨部门协同调度，并明确支持民营企业积极参与投资，共享发展红利。（199字）
国家能源局在7月全国可再生能源电力开发建设调度会上，通报了2026年上半年可再生能源发展进展：全国可再生能源装机达24.55亿千瓦，占总装机60.7%，其中风电光伏装机约19.5亿千瓦；上半年新增装机中可再生能源占比73.9%，发电量占全国总发电量41.2%，风电光伏合计发电量占全社会用电量24.6%。会议指出行业已进入高质量发展新阶段，明确“十五五”开局三项重点任务：一是推动新型能源体系、可再生能源规划及绿证交易、新能源入市等政策落地；二是扩大绿电消费，压实消纳责任，多渠道提升新能源利用率；三是加快大型风电光伏基地及海上风电、光热、分布式等各类项目前期与建设，尽快形成实物工作量。
国家能源局于2026年7月10日印发《关于开展电力建设工程施工和监理项目负责人违规任职、现场履职不到位问题专项整治的通知》，旨在强化电力建设工程安全质量监管。文件明确：一名注册建造师在同一时期内原则上只能担任一个电力建设工程的施工项目经理；一名注册监理工程师原则上仅可担任一项监理合同的总监理工程师，确需兼任的须经建设单位书面同意且最多不超过三项，并须配备总监代表。通知还细化了例外情形（如分期施工、长期停工等），并要求健全人员任职动态核查、招投标资格审查、项目负责人变更管理及现场履职考勤等制度。同时，强调通过电力质监信息系统加强事前核查与过程监管，对违规任职、人证不符、长期离岗等行为依法依规查处。
国家能源局于2026年7月印发通知，启动全国村镇微能网建设试点工作，旨在深入推进农村能源革命。试点聚焦三类方向：一是以民生保障为主的公益性村镇微能网（群），强调“村能村用”，要求可再生能源消费比重不低于50%，新能源自发自用电量占比不低于40%；二是面向工商业负荷的综合微能网，鼓励多能互补与市场化运营，新能源自发自用电量占比不低于60%；三是边远地区智能微电网和自然灾害频发地区的应急型微电网，突出供电兜底与快速响应能力。试点分阶段推进：2028年底前建成一批示范项目，基本建立清洁能源供应与管理体系；2030年底前推广成熟经验。工作坚持政府指导、电网牵头、多方参与，实行方案申报、评估遴选、动态管理机制。（199字）
国家能源局于2026年7月20日发布公告，公布2026年6月全国新增建档立卡新能源发电项目（不含户用光伏）情况。当月共新增项目3825个，总规模以光伏发电为主：其中光伏发电项目3787个，包括集中式36个、工商业分布式3751个；风电项目32个；生物质发电项目6个。所有风电、集中式光伏及生物质发电项目清单均随公告附件一并公开，而工商业分布式光伏项目清单则通过国家可再生能源发电项目信息管理平台网站另行发布。该数据反映了当月新能源发电项目在备案登记层面的建设进展与结构分布。
文章介绍了国家能源局于2026年6月召开的全国可再生能源电力开发建设月度调度会议主要内容。截至2026年4月底，我国可再生能源总装机达24亿千瓦，占全国电力总装机的60.5%；其中风电和光伏合计装机19.11亿千瓦（光伏12.50亿千瓦），发电量占全社会用电量的24.1%。会议肯定了新能源发展总体态势良好，同时围绕“十五五”开局目标，提出七项重点工作：强化新能源并网消纳能力；推动就地就近消纳与绿电直连；加快大型基地项目建设；精准落实配套政策；完善适应高比例新能源的市场机制；提升企业全链条综合竞争力；加强跨部门、跨层级统筹协同。会议强调需多方合力保障可再生能源高质量发展。（199字）

title: 有关使用钢边框光伏组件的几点思考-索比光伏网
content:
为什么要使用钢边框光伏组件？
o 降低光伏组件的成本。组件使用钢边框，每瓦大约能节省 2 分钱人民币，1GW 光伏电站，可节省 2000 万 人民币。
o 钢材料的屈服强度、抗拉强度等都明显高于铝合金材料；钢边框组件正面和背面的静压承载力 （7200Pa/4200Pa），明显高于铝边框组件的国家标准。
o 钢边框具有更好的抗划伤特性，适合风沙大的沙戈荒地区。
o 闭口型钢边框的安装孔距和安装方式，与铝边框组件的一样或非常接近，不会降低组件的安装效率。
o 钢边框与组件支架紧密连接，形成一个整体的接地网，无需额外安装组件间的接地连线，具有接地阻抗
低、安装时长短、安装费用少等优点。
为什么钢边框光伏组件现在才被大规模采用？
o 钢材料 25 年防腐生锈问题和困扰，被锌铝镁钢材完全解决。
o 可以满足组件对边框的精度要求。某些钢边框企业的辊压成型工艺和自动化产线，生产的钢边框，可以媲 美铝边框的各类精度指标，并达到规模化的生产能力。
o 从 2025 年上半年开始，光伏电站投资方和 EPC 公司开始逐步接受钢边框组件，并在大型地面光伏电站， 特别是在沙戈荒地区广泛应用，效果卓然。
如何采购和使用钢边框光伏组件？需要注意的一些问题
o 由于钢边框组件被光伏电站业主和 EPC 公司逐步接纳和使用，近来国内涌现出不少钢边框企业，产品也五 花八门，各有特点。主要区别在原材料厂家、产品结构（截面结构）、材料厚度与锌铝镁镀层、产品精 度、产品技术参数、产能和交货能力、产品质量（产品一致性）、组件产线的组框适配性和良品率、组件 安装方式和安装效率等方面。
o 钢边框的截面构造，分为开口型和闭口型钢边框。闭口型钢边框的截面，与铝边框非常类似，即有一个闭 合的腔体来保证边框的强度。开口型，没有闭合的腔体，制成的组件的强度参数相对较弱，特别是导致电 池片隐裂的抗扭性参数。
o 钢边框的重要技术参数，为正压、背压、抗扭性和抗撕裂性，与之对应，有相应的测试方法和测试结果。
o 锌铝镁钢材料制成。钢厂的生产工艺和锌铝镁镀层（厚度与成分比）的不同，会导致锌铝镁钢材质量参差 不齐，致使防腐能力和美观度有很大差异，应尽量采用宝武钢铁集团原材料制成的钢边框。o 钢边框材料厚度。开口型钢边框，由于没有闭合的腔体结构，必须使用 1 – 1.2mm 厚度的材料，以保证能通过组件的各类疲劳和压力测试。闭口型钢边框的腔体结构更加稳定，只需要 0.6mm 厚度的材料，制成的 钢边框更加精美，精度也更高。
o 光伏组件产线的适配性。组件产线中的自动组框设备，是按照铝边框的结构特点进行设计和安装的。因为闭口型截面结构与铝边框高度相似，所以产线适配性最好，基本不影响组件生产效率，也能保证组件的良品率。开口型，与铝边框结构完全不同，导致产线适配性较差，需要对组件产线进行改造，以保证生产效 率，避免交货延误。
o 工程安装的便利性和安装效率。闭口型钢边框与铝边框高度相似，所以安装的便利性和效率差别很小，可 以忽略不计。S 型开口钢边框，其与支架固定的螺丝或压块安装面，朝向组件外侧，与铝边框完全相反， 大大增加安装难度，降低安装效率。
o 闭口型钢边框的闭合方式。闭口型钢边框有闭合的腔体，但不同厂家的腔体闭合方式完全不同，会直接影响组件的强度参数，特别是抗扭性和抗撕裂能力。现行的闭口型钢边框有三种闭合方式， A 面多层堆叠 咬合， A 面多层堆叠咬合加上 B 面焊接， C 面 6 层堆叠咬合加上多点铆压。

title: JFE Engineering and Akita Maritime Service secure offshore maintenance contract
content:
JFE Engineering and Akita Maritime Service have formed a joint venture
that has been awarded a contract to provide inspection and maintenance
services for the balance of plant (BOP) infrastructure at the offshore
wind project located off the coast of Oga City, Katagami City and Akita
The scope covers the onshore substation, onshore transmission lines, submarine
cables and monopile foundations. The initial contract will run for five
years, with the companies expected to support the assets throughout the
project's operating life through contract extensions and renewals.
The offshore wind farm is scheduled to begin operations in June 2028 and
is set to be the first project commissioned under Japan's offshore wind
development framework established under the Renewable Energy Sea Area Use
JFE Engineering said the award builds on its experience in wind farm EPC
and maintenance services, as well as its role manufacturing and transporting
monopile foundations.
According to the announcement Akita Maritime Service will provide support
including transmission line inspections and vessel coordination for maintenance
activities.

title: Semco Maritime and PTSC M&C awarded offshore substation supply contract for Fengmiao II
content:
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners has announced that the Fengmiao II offshore
wind project has signed an offshore substation supply contract with Semco
Maritime and PTSC Mechanical & Construction (PTSC M&C).
Fengmiao II is being developed by Copenhagen Offshore Partners. The 600
MW offshore wind project is located 40 kilometres off the coast of Taichung
City, Taiwan.
According to the announcement, the contract covers the engineering, procurement,
fabrication and installation of the offshore substation.
The engineering, procurement and installation of the substation's electrical
systems have been awarded to Semco Maritime, while PTSC M&C will fabricate
the offshore substation's structural components.
Mark Wainwright, CEO of the Fengmiao II Offshore Wind Project, said: "Through
our collaboration on Fengmiao I, both teams have established a strong working
relationship and a high level of mutual understanding while gaining valuable
engineering experience."
Adding: "These achievements provide a solid foundation for the successful
delivery of the Fengmiao II offshore substation."
Naiwen Marina Hsu, president of CIP Asia-Pacific, said: "Fengmiao
II will build on the success of Fengmiao I by continuing to leverage its
proven development model, with financial close targeted by the end of the
second quarter of 2027."

title: Seaway 7 installs first inter-array cable at Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm
content:
Seaway 7 has announced the installation of the first inter-array cable
for the 2.9 GW Hornsea
3 offshore wind farm.
The Ørsted led project is located 120 km off the Norfolk coast and will
generate enough renewable electricity to power an estimated 3.3 million
UK households.
The company will carry out the transport and installation of 536 km of
66 kV inter-array cables, helping connect the wind farm's 231 offshore
wind turbines to the offshore converter station.
According to the announcement, Seaway 7's work on the Hornsea 3 project
continues its long-term relationship with Ørsted, following their involvement
in the 1.2 GW Hornsea 1 and 1.3 GW Hornsea 2 offshore wind farms.

title: SSEN Transmission successfully uses drones to install DLR technology
content:
SSEN Transmission has announced the successful use of a drone to install
Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) technology on a live transmission conductor,
marking a milestone as the first company in the UK to complete the process.
an outage or physical access to the line.
According to the announcement, the method will help maximise network capacity,
as DLR uses real-time environmental conditions to calculate how much electricity
a transmission line can safely carry, rather than relying on predetermined
seasonal limits.
Niall McDonald, SSEN Transmission Project Director, said: “This approach
has the potential to make it easier and more flexible to deploy DLR across
our network, helping us make better use of existing capacity and move more
renewable electricity through the system.”
Martin Queen, Chief Engineer at Ofgem, the energy regulator, said: “A
live-line installation is exceptionally important because it allows us
to avoid system outages, which are becoming increasingly difficult to accommodate
on a highly constrained network.”

title: Acta Marine completes four vessel CSOV newbuild programme
content:
Acta Marine has announced the delivery of its latest next-generation Walk-to-Work
(W2W) DP2 Construction Service Operation Vessel (CSOV), Acta Aquarius,
following Acta Pegasus, Acta Hercules and Acta Gemini. Acta Marine confirmed
this is the final vessel in the series.
Rob Boer, CEO of Acta Marine, commented: "The delivery of Acta Aquarius
is a proud moment for Acta Marine and marks the completion of our four
vessel newbuild programme with Tersan Shipyard."
Adding: "These vessels represent an important investment in the future
of our fleet and strengthen our ability to support our clients in the offshore
wind industry."
The new vessel is powered by dual-fuel methanol, supporting lower-emission
operations. According to the company, it also features a telescopic motion
compensated gangway and a 3D motion compensated crane.
According to the announcement, Acta Marine will look to deploy the vessel
in support of offshore wind operations.

title: The Controversial AI Interpretability Research that Caught Sam Altman’s Eye
content: During OpenAI’s talks in recent months with AI startup Goodfire over a possible acquisition or partnership—discussions my colleagues and I reported this morning—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was particularly interested in the work of Nick Cammarata , a onetime OpenAI researcher now at Goodfire who has made waves recently with new claims about how AI thinks. Cammarata published an essay last month and a follow-up report last week that have caused quite a stir among AI researchers—with some applauding it as a potential breakthrough in our ability to understand AI models and others dismissing it as hype. The reaction goes to show that some areas of AI research are still so immature that scientists don’t even agree on what counts as good research—a fact that hasn’t prevented billion-dollar valuations for startups based on unproven AI technology. Goodfire’s research specialty is known as mechanistic interpretability , or mech interp for short, which seeks to understand the inner workings of AI models rather than just their outward behavior. AI models are made of trillions of numbers, making them “black boxes” that a person can’t understand the way a programmer can simply read the lines of code in traditional software. As a result, it’s tricky to know how an AI model will act in new situations and to understand mistakes when they occur. Cammarata’s essay, titled Neural Networks Are Already Clean , argued that the artificial “neurons” in AI models—mathematical functions built on those trillions of numbers—could actually be easier to understand than researchers had previously thought. As a result, his argument goes, the outlook for startups like Goodfire that aim to explain how AI models work is more promising. For example, back in 2017 mech interp researchers found a neuron inside an AI image model that seemed to light up when the model was looking at an image of a car or a cat. Most neurons seemed to perform multiple unrelated jobs like this, confounding the researchers who tried to study them. In fact, in 2023, when Cammarata was working at OpenAI, he tried using OpenAI’s GPT-4 model to make sense of the neurons in a GPT-2 model, and found that it could only explain 1.7% of the neurons—at most. But thanks to improvements in training models and techniques to interpret them, the picture is no longer hopeless, Cammarata argues. About 90% of the neurons in Alibaba’s Qwen3-32B have just one job, making them possible to understand. And when Cammarata revisited the car-and-cat neuron, he realized that cat faces and the corner of a car share a similar V-shape, which is what the neuron was actually picking up on. “The story of interpretability, as I see it, has largely been one of finding out that what was under the microscope was better than we thought,” he wrote. “The microscope just wasn’t tuned right, and what needed tuning was often pretty subtle.” Several prominent mech interp researchers were not as convinced by Cammarata’s essay. They commented that his research direction was promising but he was exaggerating the significance of the results. Neel Nanda , who leads Google DeepMind’s work on mech interp, wrote on social media that Cammarata’s essay “is interesting work, but I don‘t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability.” The essay overestimates how much neurons are understood, Nanda wrote, and even if every neuron was understood, a lot of questions about how a model works would remain unanswered. OpenAI researcher Leo Gao also weighed in, writing a rebuttal to Cammarata titled “ Neural networks are not already clean ” in which he countered that Cammarata’s essay is “nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously anticipated.” Liv Gorton , who previously worked at Goodfire and now works at Anthropic , tried to replicate some of Cammarata’s experiments and found different results. She also pointed out that cats’ faces are not all that V-shaped, and the neuron in question does not respond to plenty of more V-shaped images, such as bird beaks. Cammarata acknowledged the wide variety of reactions to his essay but offered a note of unity. When it comes to interpreting AI models, he wrote , “I think the problem is solvable, whether the simple thing works, it mostly works but we need some new things, or we need big new ideas. I think we can figure it out.” Here’s what else is going on… People on the Move Confidantes of Jensen Huang are informally seeking to reinstate him as Nvidia’s CEO and encouraging him to fight to reclaim his old job. Meanwhile, a petition signed by some Nvidia employees is urging its board to reinstate Huang. Huang has agreed to testify under oath to Congress before Thanksgiving. title: OpenAI Explored $5 Billion–Plus Acquisition of Startup That Decodes How AI ‘Thinks’
content: As OpenAI staff this summer scrambled to understand how its AI caused security breaches inside and outside the company, leaders including CEO Sam Altman spoke multiple times with Goodfire, an Anthropic-backed startup whose technology aims to figure out why AI models behave the way they do and how to prevent them from going rogue. At one point, a senior OpenAI executive floated the idea of buying the two-year-old startup for more than $5 billion or forming another kind of business partnership, according to two people familiar with the proposal. That price would have represented a steep premium to Goodfire’s private valuation of $1.25 billion in a financing it announced in February. No deal to buy the startup was struck, but the conversations, which haven’t previously been reported, show how a once-obscure corner of the industry is getting newfound attention as AI-powered security breaches skyrocket and staff at Anthropic and OpenAI fret about their companies’ ability to control the technology they’re creating. One reason deal talks fizzled: Executives at Goodfire believe the company will be more valuable than that figure if it remains independent, as it could sell technology to multiple AI developers, according to one of the people. Goodfire says its software is becoming particularly useful as leaders at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have acknowledged that traditional forms of monitoring AI behavior are becoming less reliable. Its approach differs from the conventional method used by developers such as OpenAI: reading their AI models’ chains of thought—the text that models produce as they reason through problems—and closely watching the actions the AI actually takes. (Watch an interview with the Goodfire CEO below.) Advances in AI such as loop transformers could be contributing to that monitorability issue by reducing the amount of information models write in their chains of thought. Developing stronger safeguards has become critical to OpenAI and other model developers in recent months, in the wake of AI-related security incidents including the infamous Hugging Face breach, which OpenAI’s technology caused. (The technology also breached and took over some of OpenAI’s own systems.) OpenAI, Anthropic and others must now guard against the possibility of large legal liabilities or prosecution if their technology breaks into corporate or government systems and causes economic losses. Goodfire’s specialty is mechanistic interpretability, often referred to as mech interp. Unlike chain-of-thought monitoring, software from Goodfire and rivals like Martian looks at the mathematical computations running inside a model. The approach is not yet as advanced as the chain-of-thought approach, Goodfire admits. And some AI researchers view it as less scientifically rigorous than other forms of machine-learning research. But Goodfire co-founder and chief scientist Tom McGrath said on The Information’s AI Deep Dive that the startup expects its methods to improve rapidly and be far cheaper than chain-of-thought monitoring, which requires an AI developer to run a large language model to read another model’s chain of thought. He said he expects interpretability-based monitoring to catch up to chain-of-thought monitoring within the next six months. The San Francisco startup sells annual subscription licenses to businesses and charges for use of a product called Silico, which provides AI agents that can autonomously carry out research experiments such as finding a way to detect whether a model might be trying to perform a cyberattack. Its customers have included Rakuten and AI neuroscience company Prima Mente. Goodfire has been generating revenue, though it’s not clear how much. Because mechanistic interpretability often requires extensive access to the numbers, or weights, that make up an AI model and model developers guard this information carefully, some of Goodfire’s employees work at customers’ offices. During OpenAI’s discussions with Goodfire, Altman was especially interested in the work of Goodfire researcher Nick Cammarata, according to one of the people. Cammarata, who previously worked at OpenAI, published a viral essay last month, “ Neural Networks Are Already Clean ,” which argued that mech interp has made it easier to understand the billions of so-called neurons, the mathematical functions that make up an AI model, than researchers in the field previously thought. This understanding could help developers build better models, some researchers believe. Several of the major model developers employ researchers who focus on mech interp, although Anthropic, which helped pioneer the mech interp field, has been particularly vocal about the topic. Chris Olah, who is often credited with starting the field of mech interp, co-founded Anthropic after leaving OpenAI in 2020 and now leads interpretability work at the Claude maker. Last year, it invested $1 million in Goodfire , Anthropic’s first ever direct stake in another startup. CEO Dario Amodei said in a statement at the time that the move “reflects our belief that mechanistic interpretability is among the best bets to help us transform black-box neural networks into understandable, steerable systems.” OpenAI is hiring interpretability researchers , according to its job posts, and earlier this year it began using interpretability techniques as part of its safety processes to detect misbehavior, such as AI models responding to potentially harmful requests regarding cyberattacks or biological weapons. OpenAI researchers are becoming more enthusiastic about working on interpretability, according to someone close to the company.

title: Nvidia’s Earnings on Deck; Anthropic’s Public Debut
content: If life was simple, the biggest question this week for people in tech would be where Anthropic shares open when the AI firm goes public. (Above $150 a share? See below.) Instead, we can’t rule out that more news breaks in the Nvidia drama and overwhelms Anthropic’s week in the sun. That news could be anything from reports of other women who had affairs with the now-departed CEO, Jensen Huang to developments in the campaign to bring him back. Huang, meanwhile, has agreed to testify before Congress, which could happen this week. Of course, even without such developments, Nvidia will be in the news. The AI chip designer on Tuesday is scheduled to report earnings for its third fiscal quarter, ending in late October. Those earnings will remind us all of why it is such a star company: It has projected revenue growth of around 89%, continuing a reacceleration of growth this fiscal year from last year’s “slowdown” (when revenue grew 66%). What we’ll be focused on more than the numbers will be comments from Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress. While as finance chief she’s a fixture on these calls, on Tuesday she makes her first public appearance in charge of the company since Huang’s exit. She’s likely to address the upheaval in some way, in an effort to reassure anxious investors as best she can. Nvidia stock closed Friday at $162.85, down 13% for the week and off 32% since early October. As we’ve written , there are lots of questions about what impact Huang’s exit will have on Nvidia’s business. Those unknowns make investors uneasy. HSBC downgraded the stock to a “hold” on Friday, citing the increase in “long-term uncertainty.” You have to wonder how Nvidia’s revenue will be affected if, as seems likely, the company has to clamp down harder on smuggling of its chips to China. Huang’s ties to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang fueled billions of dollars in sales of those chips to China, as we reported . (We’d love to be a fly on the wall when President Donald Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, meet this week at their summit , by the way: Will the topic of chip smuggling come up?) Then there’s a question about all the investments Nvidia made under Huang’s oversight in neoclouds and other firms, to ensure demand for its chips remained robust. What is the real level of demand for Nvidia’s chips, assuming the smuggling-into-China route has been closed off properly and assuming Nvidia wasn’t juicing demand by investing in buyers? Answering that question is key to understanding what the company’s future growth looks like. Anthropic's Big Day Anthropic’s public debut is the other big story of the week. By all accounts, demand is intense for the offering, suggesting the IPO will price above the preliminary range of $70 to $78 a share, which represents a valuation of $1.26 trillion to $1.4 trillion. A valuation of $1.5 trillion seems more likely. To get there, Anthropic would price at $84 to $85 a share. Let’s assume that happens. It still leaves plenty of room for enthusiastic traders to bid the stock up. In fact, we’d bet it opens trading at well above $100 a share, possibly above $150. Of course, what really matters is where it trades over the next few weeks. There are some who believe Anthropic will quickly become the most valuable company in the world. Right now, Apple holds that position with a market capitalization of around $5.2 trillion. For Anthropic to pass that number, its shares would have to rise to above $288 a piece. Will it get there and if so, how quickly? (Here are details of Anthropic’s marketing event on Friday at JP Morgan Chase’s headquarters.) title: Exclusive: Three Veterans of Tesla’s Autopilot Team Got a $1 Billion Valuation for a Simulation Startup
content: For two years, Ian Glow managed Tesla’s computer simulation unit, leading a team of gamers who created the ultradetailed equivalent of high-end videogames to help train the automaker’s core new products—self-driving cars and humanoid robots. But in 2022, Glow left the company, wanting to “move faster than was possible” at Tesla to develop virtual modeling tools that he thought were essential to any effort to safely commercialize either technology. Today, Glow is CEO of simulation software startup Zeromatter, which he said has developed a model that reliably replicates aspects of the real world, such as dangerous driving conditions and the use of tools in a factory. Glow, speaking for the first time publicly about Zeromatter, said he is selling such software to companies making self-driving cars, drones and robots. He declined to disclose the startup’s revenue, but last year he raised $110 million in a Series B round that valued Zeromatter at $1.1 billion. In all, Zeromatter has raised $160 million, including two prior rounds. The emergence of the startup reflects a spillover of technology developed in the electric vehicle industry, and specifically at Tesla. Industry veterans say Tesla’s arrival in China drove the development of that country’s EV, materials and robotics supply chains, which today dominate the global EV, battery and robotics industries. In the West, Tesla, with its Optimus robot, has driven a boom in the development of humanoids. Glow co-founded Zeromatter in 2023 with two former senior managers on Tesla’s simulation team—Axel Gneiting, now chief engineer at Zeromatter, and Michael Hosticka, the startup’s head of content strategy. Today the company has a staff of more than 130 people, including some 40 other Tesla veterans. Beyond the Tesla veterans, Glow said he has recruited roughly 10 people from General Motors’ former self-driving division, Cruise, and others from Amazon’s autonomous ride-hailing unit, Zoox, as well as Boeing, Airbus and Lockheed Martin. All three co-founders were videogame developers before working for Tesla. Glow said he was drawn to Tesla because his prior job working on Minecraft in Microsoft’s Mojang Studios was too slow. He said building a simulated world to develop a self-driving car is basically the same as creating one in which humans pretend they are fighting intergalactic aliens. “The idea that you can leverage your game background to actually make robots and drones and planes and a lot of things better was really exciting to me,” Glow said. “You just make a virtual world, and instead of having a human play it, you have an AI play it, or you have some kind of controlled algorithm play it.” Still, what he was doing at Tesla was small potatoes compared with the potential. The idea for Zeromatter centers on safety and reliability: Before a company ever deploys a moving product, that product can be tried out literally a million different ways through a simulator so there is no glitch in actual use. If it’s done right, simulation software, he said, “can accelerate every self-driving car company, every aerospace company, every drone company, anyone who’s building a sensor—anyone, I mean, even in robotics.” There is a term for reaching a real-world approximation of a situation: the sim-to-real ratio. The closer you get to the real side, the more street cred your simulation model has. To get there, you need to check it against the real world, which means comparing the simulation with high-quality data for the actions of a real robot or an actual driving situation. Zeromatter has its own EVs, robots, labs and AI computing power. For example, to ensure the company’s simulation of a camera is realistic, Glow said he buys a real camera, sets it up in a lab, and uses it in a bunch of different shots with various settings, including any defects or miscalibration that can happen. Then his team reproduces all of those scenarios within a simulation tool. “We make sure that it behaves exactly like it would in the real world,” he said. Humanoids are among the toughest challenges. Glow thinks robot developers have solved locomotion—the ability to walk, dance, run and so on. Simulation can help robots get their hands working right—a trickier proposition. “You have to continue to push the physical fidelity into manipulation,” he said. “When you make all that training data, it’s going to roughly represent what's happening in the real world,” he said. “There’s [otherwise] no easy way to test to make sure [that] ‘Yeah, does my self-driving car stop at a stop sign?’ or ‘Can my robot arm actually install this part in this vehicle?’” ------ Noteworthy A U.S. ban on Chinese components is making it far more expensive for drone makers outside China to power their aircraft—about four times as expensive. That’s according to Qichao Hu, CEO of U.S. drone battery maker SES AI, who told me Chinese drone batteries cost about 70 cents per ampere-hour, compared with around $3 for drone batteries made outside China. Hu said China’s cheaper materials largely account for the cost difference. But U.S. government purchasing rules mean this wide pricing gulf doesn’t hurt business for SES and other non-Chinese battery makers, he suggested. Those rules exclude Chinese components, including batteries, in drones purchased by the Pentagon. Enovix showed last week that the drone boom goes only so far in terms of reviving the fortunes of struggling U.S. next-generation battery startups. Last month, we reported that Enovix had landed its first commercial revenue in a big drone battery sale. Last Thursday, Enovix highlighted that news in its third-quarter earnings call, saying it was doubling down on drones by turning its near-term focus largely to making batteries for the aircraft and the significant revenue that business generates. While that announcement was well and good, several analysts on the call had questions about another disclosure, which was that Enovix was putting its prior main ambition—making lucrative smartphone batteries—on the back burner. Investors had been counting on that smartphone revenue.
