Eine aktuelle Studie der Technischen Universität Dresden (TUD) untersucht erstmals die volkswirtschaftlichen Kosten verpflichtender Gesundheits-Checks für Autofahrerinnen und Autofahrer ab 65 Jahren. Die Modellrechnung zeigt: Durch die Einführung solcher Untersuchungen in Deutschland würden langfristig rund 540.000 Menschen ihren Führerschein verlieren – mit erheblichen gesellschaftlichen Folgen. Die Forschenden plädieren daher für eine differenzierte Bewertung altersabhängiger Führerscheinuntersuchungen.
Mit dem demografischen Wandel steigt die Zahl älterer Menschen, die aktiv am Straßenverkehr teilnehmen. In der öffentlichen und politischen Debatte zur Verkehrssicherheit wird immer wieder über verpflichtende Gesundheits-Checks für ältere Autofahrerinnen und Autofahrer diskutiert. Eine aktuelle Studie von Verkehrswirtschaftswissenschaftlern der TUD untersucht am Beispiel eines Modells für Deutschland die Folgen altersabhängiger Gesundheits-Checks ganzheitlich und nimmt dabei auch die gesellschaftlichen Effekte in den Blick.
Die Forschenden modellierten dafür ein Verfahren, wie es in verschiedenen europäischen Ländern praktiziert wird: Ab dem 65. Lebensjahr müssten Autofahrerinnen und Autofahrer alle fünf Jahre eine verpflichtende ärztliche Untersuchung bei ihrer Hausärztin oder ihrem Hausarzt absolvieren. Die angenommenen Kosten pro Untersuchung betragen 25 Euro. Die Modellrechnungen zeigen, dass bei einer Einführung solcher Gesundheits-Checks in Deutschland langfristig rund drei Prozent der über 65-Jährigen ihren Führerschein dauerhaft verlieren würden. Das entspricht etwa 540.000 Menschen.
Mehr als nur Untersuchungskosten
Eine volkswirtschaftliche Kosten-Nutzen-Analyse geht jedoch weit über die unmittelbaren Ausgaben für die Untersuchungen hinaus. Sie macht unterschiedliche gesellschaftliche Auswirkungen vergleichbar, indem sie diese in Geldwerten ausdrückt. Dazu gehören beispielsweise vermiedene Unfallschäden und eingesparte Autokosten, aber auch die Folgen eines Führerscheinentzugs: der Verlust persönlicher Unabhängigkeit, eingeschränkte soziale Teilhabe und das Risiko psychischer Belastungen durch zunehmende Isolation. „Erst wenn alle unterschiedlichen Effekte gemeinsam betrachtet werden, lässt sich beurteilen, ob eine Maßnahme aus gesellschaftlicher Sicht tatsächlich vorteilhaft ist“, erklärt Tano Kannegiesser, wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter an der Professur für Volkswirtschaftslehre (Verkehrspolitik und Raumwirtschaft) und Erstautor der Studie.
Unfallrisiko als entscheidender Faktor
Ob die Bilanz am Ende positiv oder negativ ausfällt, hängt in den Berechnungen entscheidend von einem Faktor ab: Wie stark sinkt das durchschnittliche Unfallrisiko der älteren Autofahrerinnen und Autofahrer, die den Test bestehen und weiterfahren dürfen? Zwar gehen Unfälle rein rechnerisch schon dadurch zurück, dass Menschen ohne Führerschein nicht mehr fahren – doch das eigentliche Ziel der Checks ist es, gezielt besonders unsichere Fahrerinnen und Fahrer herauszufiltern.
Den Modellrechnungen zufolge müsste das durchschnittliche Unfallrisiko der verbleibenden Seniorinnen und Senioren um knapp zwei Prozent sinken, damit der Sicherheitsgewinn die hohen Mobilitätsverluste ausgleicht. Ein solcher Sicherheitsgewinn konnte in bisherigen wissenschaftlichen Untersuchungen für Europa jedoch nicht nachgewiesen werden.
Ohne Sicherheitsgewinn überwiegt gesellschaftlicher Schaden
Bleibt dieser zusätzliche Sicherheitseffekt tatsächlich aus, überwiegen die negativen Folgen deutlich: In der Modellrechnung beziffern die Forschenden den gesellschaftlichen Schaden auf rund 15.000 Euro pro dauerhaft entzogenem Führerschein. Hochgerechnet auf die deutsche Bevölkerung ergeben sich daraus – bei jährlich ca. 50.000 entzogenen Führerscheinen – volkswirtschaftliche Kosten von rund 760 Millionen Euro pro Jahr.
Die Forschenden warnen deshalb vor einer pauschalen Übernahme der Europäischen Praxis: „Deutschland sollte altersmedizinische Tests nach europäischem Vorbild nur Einführen, wenn deren Wirksamkeit eindeutig nachgewiesen werden kann. Die Maßnahmen sollten gezielt auf tatsächliche individuelle Risiken ausgerichtet sein und neben möglichen Sicherheitsgewinnen auch die Folgen für Mobilität und gesellschaftliche Teilhabe berücksichtigen“, fordert Kannegiesser.

Die Finalistinnen und Finalisten des Bundeswettbewerbes KI 2026 in Tübingen mit Alumni und dem BWKI Team.

Funksprüche im Katastropheneinsatz zum Lagebild ordnen, KI-Antworten in Leichte Sprache übersetzen und OP-Instrumente auf Rückstände prüfen – Teams entwickeln praxisorientierte Projekte
Johannes Nirschl, Jonas Kaindl und Alexander Kluge aus Neubiberg im Landkreis München haben am Freitag mit dem Projekt „J.A.R.“ den 1.500 Euro dotierten Hauptpreis beim diesjährigen Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz (BWKI) gewonnen. J.A.R. wandelt gesprochene Meldungen aus Katastropheneinsätzen mit einer eigens nachtrainierten Spracherkennung in Text um und ordnet sie zu einem Lagebild für die Einsatzleitung. Die Jury begeisterte die Detailtiefe des Projektes, sowie die Entwicklungsarbeit im spezifischen Anwendungsfall. Neben dem Geldpreis erhalten die Jugendlichen einen Praktikumsplatz beim Robotik- und Automationsunternehmen FANUC.
Zehn Teams aus acht Bundesländern traten am 13. November beim Finale des achten Bundeswettbewerbs Künstliche Intelligenz an. Ihre Projekte reichten von Alltagshilfen über Medizin und Katastrophenschutz bis zur Grundlagenforschung. Austragungsort war das NeckaWa in Tübingen, der Stadt, in der der Wettbewerb 2018 ins Leben gerufen wurde.
Sonderpreis „AI for Good“
Mit dem Sonderpreis „AI for Good“ für ein besonders nachhaltiges KI-Projekt wurde Magnus Schlinsog aus Potsdam für das Projekt „JACOB – KI in leichter Sprache“ ausgezeichnet. Der Preis ist mit 1.000 Euro dotiert. JACOB ist ein selbst trainiertes Sprachmodell, das Fragen in Leichter Sprache beantwortet und KI so auch für Menschen mit Lernschwierigkeiten zugänglich macht.
Sonderpreis „No Risk, No Fun!“
Den mit 750 Euro dotierten Sonderpreis „No risk, no fun!“ für die innovativste Idee oder eine außergewöhnliche Hardwarelösung erhielten Albert Heruth aus Hemmingstedt im Landkreis Dithmarschen und Jakob Rudolph aus Leipzig für das Projekt „SterilVision“. Mit Hilfe von KI prüft SterilVision chirurgische Instrumente nach der Reinigung auf Blut, Proteinreste und Kratzer und markiert auffällige Stellen für das Fachpersonal.
Online-Abstimmung für Publikumspreis
Zum Publikumsfavoriten wählten die Online-Abstimmenden Konstantin Borodulin, Peter Staykov und Dorian Benbassat aus Berlin mit dem Projekt „German Lipnet“. Der Publikumspreis ist mit 500 Euro dotiert. German LipNet liest deutsche Wörter von den Lippen ab und kombiniert Bild und Ton, sodass Wörter auch im Stimmengewirr deutlich zuverlässiger erkannt werden. Vom 3. bis 13. November konnten Interessierte auf der BWKI-Website (
https://www.bw-ki.de/
) die Finalprojekte in kurzen Erklärvideos kennenlernen und online abstimmen.
Der Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz richtet sich an Schülerinnen und Schüler weiterführender Schulen, die allein oder im Team mit bis zu vier Personen eigene KI-Projekte entwickeln, mit denen sie etwas bewirken wollen. Nach der Anmeldung im Frühjahr 2026 hatten die Teilnehmenden rund ein halbes Jahr Zeit, ihre Ideen umzusetzen. Zehn Teams qualifizierten sich für das Finale in Tübingen und stellten ihre Projekte einer interdisziplinären Jury aus Wissenschaft, Anwendung und Gesellschaft vor.
„Die Projekte der Finalistinnen und Finalisten zeigen, dass junge Menschen schon früh das Potenzial haben, Wissenschaft und Technologie verantwortungsvoll weiterzudenken und für die Gesellschaft nutzbar zu machen“, sagt Professorin Dr. Karla Pollmann, Rektorin der Universität Tübingen. „In diesem Sinne passt auch unser Leitspruch ‚Attempto – Ich wag’s’ sehr gut zum Bundeswettbewerb KI: Neues entsteht dort, wo junge Menschen den Mut haben, eigene Ideen auszuprobieren und weiterzuentwickeln.”
Neben der Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung als Hauptförderer wird der Wettbewerb von Festo, FANUC, Droemer Knaur, Cyber Valley und Amazon Future Engineer unterstützt.
Über den Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz (BWKI)
Mit dem jährlich stattfindenden BWKI sollen Schülerinnen und Schüler motiviert werden, eigene Ideen mithilfe von Künstlicher Intelligenz umzusetzen. Der Wettbewerb wurde 2018 am Tübingen AI Center – einer Forschungseinrichtung der Universität Tübingen und des Max-Planck-Instituts für Intelligente Systeme – ins Leben gerufen und ist Mitglied der AG Bundesweite Jugendwettbewerbe. Die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung ist seit 2020 Hauptförderer des BWKI. Mehr Infos unter:
https://www.bw-ki.de/
Über die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung
Die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung fördert Wissenschaft und Lehre in den MINT-Disziplinen Mathematik, Informatik, Naturwissenschaften und Technik. Als Partnerin exzellenter Wissenschaft ermöglicht sie Freiräume für Grundlagen- und anwendungsorientierte Forschung. Die Stiftung wurde 1889 von Ernst Abbe in Jena gegründet und ist heute eine der großen privaten wissenschaftsfördernden Stiftungen in Deutschland. Sie ist alleinige Eigentümerin der Carl Zeiss AG und der SCHOTT AG. Ihre Fördertätigkeit wird aus den Dividendenausschüttungen der beiden Stiftungsunternehmen finanziert.
Über das Tübingen AI Center
Der Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz ist ein Outreach-Projekt des Tübingen AI Centers. Das KI-Zentrum ist eine Einrichtung der Universität Tübingen in Kooperation mit dem Max-Planck-Institut für Intelligente Systeme, gefördert vom Forschungsministerium Baden-Württemberg und vom Bundesministerium für Bildung und Forschung. Ziel der Forschenden ist die Weiterentwicklung robuster lernender Systeme. Gleichzeitig sollen maschinelle Entscheidungsprozesse besser interpretierbar und fairer werden. Grundlagenforschung wird mit Transfer und Ausbildung verknüpft. Gemeinsam mit anderen Forschenden in Europa soll ein Beitrag für gesellschaftlich wertvolle Technologien als “AI made in Europe” geleistet werden. Mehr Informationen unter:
https://tuebingen.ai/

title: Beginn einer wundervollen Freundschaft? – Interaktion entscheidend dafür, ob Menschen Roboter akzeptieren
content:
Beginn einer wundervollen Freundschaft? – Interaktion entscheidend dafür, ob Menschen Roboter akzeptieren
Ob Menschen humanoide Roboter akzeptieren, hängt nicht nur davon ab, was sie können und für uns leisten, sondern vor allem, wie wir die Interaktion mit diesen erleben – mit all unseren Sinnen und über längere Zeit. Zu diesem Schluss kommt ein Forschungsteam der Universität Potsdam, das die psychologischen Grundlagen der Akzeptanz humanoider Roboter betrachtet hat. Über die Akzeptanz entschieden nicht allein technische Leistungsfähigkeit, Sicherheit oder die Erfüllung menschlicher Bedürfnisse.
Vielmehr entstehe diese durch ein dynamisches Zusammenspiel von Wahrnehmung und sozialer Interaktion, in dem Menschen und Roboter ihre Begegnungen wechselseitig gestalten. Die Ergebnisse ihrer theoretischen Analyse haben Katharina Kühne, Yuefang Zhou und Martin H. Fischer nun im Journal „Science Robotics“ veröffentlicht.
„Insbesondere Stimme, Berührung, Bewegungen und soziale Verhaltensweisen spielen dabei eine wichtige Rolle“, sagt Dr. Katharina Kühne, die Hauptautorin des Artikels „Through Human Eyes: How Perception and Interaction Shape Humanoid Robot Acceptance“.
Es ist also auch der „erste Eindruck“ der zählt. Und zwar ganz explizit nicht nur davon, was Roboter leisten und ob sie ihre Aufgaben erwartungsgemäß erfüllen. Entscheidend ist den Forschenden zufolge ganz wesentlich die Wahrnehmung der Roboter auf einer Ebene, auf der wir normalerweise andere Menschen wahrnehmen. Verantwortlich dafür sei vor allem der Mechanismus des Anthropomorphismus – dass wir dazu neigen, nicht-menschlichen Entitäten menschliche Eigenschaften und mentale Zustände zuzuschreiben. Dies verleite nicht zuletzt die Entwickler von Robotern dazu, ihnen immer mehr menschliche Züge zu verleihen. Dabei gebe es durchaus ein „Zuviel“, warnt Katharina Kühne: „Eine zunehmende Menschenähnlichkeit kann kontraproduktiv werden, wenn Roboter die Erwartungen der Nutzer nicht erfüllen.“ Dann entstehe statt Vertrauen eher Unbehagen und Ablehnung. Forschung zeige, dass die positivsten Reaktionen und Interaktionen eher durch „ein moderates Maß an menschenähnlichen Merkmalen“ entstehen. Das Forschungsteam plädiert deshalb für eine verkörperte („embodied“) Sicht der Mensch-Roboter-Interaktion: Wie wir Roboter bewerten und ob wir sie akzeptieren, ist nicht nur davon abhängig, was diese tun, sondern ebenso wie wir sie wahrnehmen.
Ob Roboter langfristig akzeptiert werden, hängt aber ebenso von weiteren Faktoren ab: „Auch individuelle Erfahrungen, Erwartungen und wiederholte Begegnungen beeinflussen, ob Roboter als vertrauenswürdig, sympathisch oder unheimlich wahrgenommen werden“, sagt Katharina Kühne. Wir entwickeln unser Bild von Robotern also weiter, je nachdem, welche Erfahrungen wir mit ihnen machen. „Schließlich entwickeln sich Wahrnehmungen durch wiederholte Interaktionen, was die Bedeutung langfristiger Prozesse wie der Habituation bzw. Vertrautmachung unterstreicht“, so die Forscherin. „Interaktive Erfahrungen sind die primären Treiber von Mensch-Roboter-Beziehungen. Sie formen iterativ die Erwartungen, das Vertrauen und die langfristige Akzeptanz der Nutzenden.“
Der Artikel online:

Vorrichtung und Verfahren zur kontinuierlichen Plasma-Funktionalisierung kleiner Partikel, Pulver und Fasern im nm- und µm-Maßstab für die Industrie.
Die beiden Forschungseinrichtungen INNOVENT e.V. und SKZ - KFE gGmbH mit dem Europäischen Zentrum für Dispersionstechnologien (EZD) haben im Rahmen des von der IGF geförderten Projektes „Kontinuierliche Plasmabehandlung von Pulvern für den optimierten Einsatz in flüssigen Matrices – KoPla optiMa“ eine Methode zur kontinuierlichen Oberflächenbehandlung von Pulvern unter Verwendung von atmosphärischen Plasmen sowie eine prozessbegleitende Methode zur Bestimmung der Pulverbenetzbarkeit entwickelt.
Für die Bereitstellung wirtschaftlich nachhaltiger funktionaler Oberflächen stehen zunehmend Materialkombinationen im Fokus von Forschung und Produktion. Beschichtungen aus Dispersionen wie Suspensionen und Slurries ermöglichen die Verbindung sich ergänzender positiver Materialeigenschaften für neue Anwendungsmöglichkeiten.
Grundlegende Bedingung für die Herstellung stabiler Dispersionen ist eine gute und langzeitstabile Verteilung der Partikel, Pulver bzw. Fasern in der Flüssigkeit. Das wird insbesondere bei der Verwendung nachhaltiger Dispersionsmedien auf Wasserbasis zu einer großen Herausforderung.
Diesem Problem hat sich das Projektteam gestellt. Für die Optimierung von Dispergier-Prozessen wurde von INNOVENT e.V. eine Vorrichtung zur plasmagestützten kontinuierlichen Pulverfunktionalisierung entwickelt. Anwendungsbeispiele sind u.a. die Aktivierung niedrig-energetischer Materialien wie Polymere für die Dispergierung in Wasser. So können umweltschädliche Chemikalien als Dispergierhilfsmittel für industriell notwendige Prozesse ersetzt werden.
Herzstück der Vorrichtung ist eine flächige Plasmaquelle. Plasma – der 4. Aggregatzustand der Materie – besteht aus energetisch angeregten Elektronen und Ionen. Die im Plasma gebündelte Energie wird zur Funktionalisierung von Oberflächen genutzt. Dabei sind Prozesse wie Feinstreinigung, Aktivierung/energetische Anregung, Ätzprozesse und die Abscheidung von Nano-Beschichtungen etabliert. Diese Wirkung kann auch für die Funktionalisierung von kleinsten Partikeln, Pulvern und Fasern mit einem besonders hohen Oberflächen-Volumen-Verhältnis eingesetzt werden.
Im Gegensatz zu gegenwärtig auf dem Markt befindlichen Systemen zur Pulverfunktionalisierung arbeitet die neue Vorrichtung kontinuierlich mit einem Durchsatz von derzeit ungefähr 50 g/h pro Plasma-Array, allerdings ist die Anzahl der eingesetzten Plasmaquellen nach oben skalierbar. Es können verschiedenste Partikel, Pulver und Fasern basierend beispielsweise auf Polymeren, Keramiken, Glas, Holz, Kompositen oder Farbstoffen funktionalisiert werden. Auch bei UHMW-Polymeren wurde durch die Plasmabehandlung eine Oberflächenmodifizierung nachgewiesen.
Die Entwicklung der Plasma-Funktionalisierungs-Vorrichtung und des Verfahrens war Schwerpunkt der Projektarbeit bei INNOVENT e.V.
Die Vorrichtung kann für eine Pulverfunktionalisierung als Dienstleistung für Anwendungen in vielen Industriebereichen eingesetzt werden. Mehrere wirtschaftliche Fallbeispiele wie die Abscheidung von Dispersionsschichten nach den Verfahren der Plasmachemischen Oxidation und der Chemisch Nickel-Oberflächenveredelung, die Funktionalisierung von Polymerpartikeln für den 3D-Druck, die Behandlung von Füllstoffen für Kompositwerkstoffe und die antimikrobielle Behandlung von kleinen Partikeln, Pulvern, Fasern und/oder Wirkstoffen zeigen das hohe Potenzial für die kontinuierliche Plasma-Pulverfunktionalisierung. Fertige Dispersionen der funktionalisierten Partikel, Pulver und Fasern weisen dabei in den durchgeführten Untersuchungen eine hohe Langzeitstabilität und Lagerfähigkeit auf.
Ergänzend zur Anlage zur Oberflächenaktivierung von Pulvern entwickelte das Projektteam am EZD in Selb einen Versuchsaufbau, der die Einsinkgeschwindigkeit von Pulverpartikeln in Prozessflüssigkeiten erfasst. Dieser robuste Aufbau liefert Hinweise auf die Benetzbarkeit der Pulver, die eine wichtige Voraussetzung für ihre Dispergierung in der jeweiligen Flüssigkeit darstellt. Da das Verfahren auf dem Einsinkverhalten der Partikel basiert, setzt seine Anwendung voraus, dass die Partikel eine höhere Dichte als die jeweilige Flüssigkeit aufweisen. Das Verfahren kann beispielsweise bei Wareneingangsprüfungen eingesetzt werden, um Abweichungen zwischen Pulverchargen frühzeitig zu erkennen und so zur Vermeidung von Produktionsfehlern beizutragen. Im Rahmen des Projekts lieferte der Versuchsaufbau vergleichbare Aussagen zur Benetzbarkeit wie die etablierte Washburn-Methode, welche vor allem im wissenschaftlichen Bereich Anwendung findet.

Nicht nur die chinesischen Martial-Art-Choreographien mit humanoiden Robotern lassen das Gefühl aufkommen, dass Deutschland und Europa den Wettbewerb in diesem Bereich schon längst verloren haben. Das sehen rund 70 führende deutsche Produktionswissenschaftlerinnen und -wissenschaftler jedoch ganz anders. Im Verbund der WGP haben sie ein Standpunktpapier veröffentlicht, in dem sie völlig neue Wege für die Entwicklung von humanoiden Robotern aufzeigen.
Im Blick haben sie dabei die produzierende Industrie, die sich derzeit bekanntermaßen in unruhigem Fahrwasser befindet. Ihr neues Konzept der „Humanoiden Produktionsroboter (HPR)“ könnte eine Chance sein, Deutschland und Europa wieder in eine Vorreiterposition zu katapultieren.
Als HPR definiert die WGP intelligente Roboter, die Fabrikmitarbeitende in der Produk-tion unterstützen – ein Muss angesichts von Fachkräftemangel und steigendem Pro-duktivitätsdruck. Sie zeichnen sich maßgeblich durch Steifigkeit, Genauigkeit, Tragfä-higkeit und dank entsprechender Sensorik durch umfassende Perzeption und domä-nenspezifische KI aus.
Humanoide vom Embodiment losgelöst denken
Die humanoide Ausprägung betrachten die Produktionsforschenden dabei nicht als Selbstzweck, sondern definieren sie über die auf Menschen ausgerichtete Produktionsinfrastruktur. „Wesentliche humanoide Eigenschaften sind die Umwelterkennung und daraus abgeleitete Aktionen. Die Gestalt ergibt sich aus der jeweiligen Aufgabe in der Produktion“, erläutert Prof. Jürgen Fleischer, Präsident der WGP und Leiter des wbk Instituts für Produktionstechnik am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT). Und dort spielt neben Genauigkeit bis in den Submillimeter-Bereich auch die Tragfähigkeit eine große Rolle. Schwere Bauteile oder Werkzeuge zu transportieren, fällt mit zwei Armen an einem schmalen Rumpf deutlich schwerer als mit maximal belastbaren Ar-men auf einem stabilen Flurförderzeug.
Die Forschenden beschreiben in ihrem Standpunktpapier unterschiedliche Kinematiken für definierte Aufgabenbereiche. Um die verschiedenen Modelle wirtschaftlich und schnell verfügbar zu machen, schlagen sie einen modularen Aufbau der Systeme vor, damit sie bei Bedarf schnell für neue Aufgaben umgerüstet werden können.
Das Vorgehen in der Entwicklung von Humanoiden umdrehen
Neben diesen neu zu entwickelnden HPR sollten auch bereits im Einsatz befindliche Industrieroboter aufgerüstet werden. „Die industrielle Wertschöpfung findet hierzulande überwiegend in bestehenden Fabriken statt. Die Herausforderung besteht deshalb darin, diese Robotiklösungen zu ertüchtigen, sich flexibel und wirtschaftlich in die Brownfield-Strukturen integrieren zu lassen“, betont Fleischer. „Wir müssen hierfür auch unsere hochentwickelten Roboter mit neuen Kinematiken, Sensoren und KI-Modellen ausrüsten, damit sie ihre Umwelt wahrnehmen und ihrer jeweiligen Aufgabe entsprechend situationsgerecht reagieren können.“ Die WGP grenzt sich damit von der verbreiteten Vorgehensweise ab, zunächst einen humanoiden Roboter zu entwickeln und erst danach nach Einsatzfeldern zu suchen.
Da sie mit Menschen in der Fabrik kooperieren, lenken die Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler ein besonderes Augenmerk auf die Sicherheit. Wirtschaftlichkeit wird auch unter dem Aspekt betrachtet, dass ein Wechsel der Aufgabe mit einem deutlich geringeren Aufwand verbunden sein sollte als die Implementierung einer entsprechenden Automatisierungslösung.
Es muss schnell konkret werden
„Wir verfügen in Deutschland über herausragende mechatronische Kompetenzen“, sagt der WGP-Präsident. „Wenn wir dieses Wissen mit den Möglichkeiten der KI zusammenbringen, können wir uns mit den humanoiden Produktionsrobotern auf dem Weltmarkt ein Allleinstellungsmerkmal schaffen.“ Das allerdings sei nur möglich, wenn Verbundprojekte und umfangreiche Kooperationen zustande kommen: unternehmensübergreifend und europaweit. Denn bei allen mechatronischen Kompetenzen kommen gerade bezüglich der künstlichen Intelligenz oder Rechenhardware auch Abhängigkeiten ins Spiel.
Trotzdem müsse zügig eine „koordinierte Forschungs-, Standardisierungs- und Pilotagenda“ beschlossen und mit ersten industriellen Anwendungen sichtbar gemacht werden. Das ist gerade in diesen krisengeschüttelten Zeiten, in denen es an Wagniskapital für die Skalierung mangelt, eine Herausforderung. Aber die 70 Professorinnen und Professoren sind sich sicher, dass dies eine dringend notwendige Investition in die Zukunft des Industriestandorts Deutschland ist, um den Trend der Deindustrialisierung zu stoppen und den Wohlstand für die Zukunft zu sichern. „Wenn wir mit den HPR in den kommenden zwei bis drei Jahren substantiell vorankommen“, so das Fazit von Fleischer, „dann ist das für Deutschland die Chance, die Weltspitze in diesem Bereich einzunehmen.“

Die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung fördert über ihr „Wildcard“-Programm ab dem kommenden Jahr zwei Forschungsprojekte der Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz mit insgesamt rund 767.000 Euro. Wie die Stiftung in der vergangenen Woche bekanntgab, handelt es sich dabei um die Projekte „Spin-Selective Chiral Nanoscale Cooling (NanoCool)“ und „MeasurIng room tempeRAture high-frequency maGnEtic quantum effects in solids (MIRAGE)“.
Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung fördert zwei Forschungsprojekte der JGU
Die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung (CZS) fördert über ihr „Wildcard“-Programm ab dem kommenden Jahr zwei Forschungsprojekte der Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz (JGU) mit insgesamt rund 767.000 Euro. Wie die Stiftung in der vergangenen Woche bekanntgab, handelt es sich dabei um die Projekte „Spin-Selective Chiral Nanoscale Cooling (NanoCool)“ und „MeasurIng room tempeRAture high-frequency maGnEtic quantum effects in solids (MIRAGE)“. Mit dem Programm „Wildcard“ unterstützt die CZS interdisziplinäre Konsortien aus jeweils drei bis fünf Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftlern, die unkonventionelle Ideen mit hohem Innovationspotenzial im MINT-Bereich (Mathematik, Informatik, Naturwissenschaften und Technik) verfolgen.
Das Projekt „Spin-Selective Chiral Nanoscale Cooling” (NanoCool)
Die Wärmeentwicklung wird zunehmend zum begrenzenden Faktor für leistungsfähigere Computer und den Fortschritt der künstlichen Intelligenz. Herkömmliche Kühlsysteme stoßen insbesondere dort an ihre Grenzen, wo auf Computerchips winzige Bereiche besonders heiß werden. Das Projekt NanoCool verfolgt deshalb einen völlig neuen Ansatz: Es nutzt den Spin von Elektronen, eine quantenphysikalische Eigenschaft, die Elektronen wie winzige Magnete wirken lässt. Fließt elektrischer Strom durch chirale Moleküle, die sich durch eine besondere räumliche Struktur auszeichnen, können die Spins gezielt ausgerichtet werden. Durch diese sogenannte Spinpolarisation und den anschließenden Verlust der Ausrichtung kann Wärme abgegeben, beziehungsweise aufgenommen werden. Die Moleküle könnten so wie winzige Wärmepumpen wirken. NanoCool will dieses Prinzip untersuchen und für die gezielte Kühlung direkt auf Computerchips nutzbar machen, ohne Magnete oder bewegliche Teile. Damit könnte das Projekt den Weg für eine neue Generation leistungsfähigerer und energieeffizienterer KI-Hardware ebnen.
Von der JGU sind Prof. Dr. Eva Rentschler, vom Department Chemie, als Sprecherin und Prof. Dr. Angela Wittmann, vom Institut für Physik, beteiligt. Ergänzt wird das Team durch Prof. Dr. Yossi Paltiel, Professor für Angewandte Physik an der Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Die CZS fördert das Projekt von Februar 2027 bis Januar 2029 mit 894.000 Euro. Zirka 654.000 Euro davon fließen an die JGU.
Das Projekt „MeasurIng room tempeRAture high-frequency maGnEtic quantum effects in solids (MIRAGE)”
Die Informationstechnologie steht vor einer grundlegenden Geschwindigkeitslücke: Während Glasfasernetze Daten bereits mit mehreren Terabit pro Sekunde übertragen, bleibt die elektronische Verarbeitung auf Gigahertz-Frequenzen beschränkt. MIRAGE will diese Lücke schließen und eine ultraschnelle, energieeffiziente Quanteninformationsplattform entwickeln, die mit optischer Kommunikation kompatibel ist. Dazu nutzt das Projekt kollektive Spin-Anregungen, sogenannte Magnonen, als Informationsträger. Diese können im Multi-Terahertz-Bereich arbeiten, ohne die Wärmeverluste herkömmlicher Elektronik zu verursachen. Ziel ist es, erstmals nachzuweisen, dass Magnonen in Festkörpern bei Raumtemperatur Quantenkorrelationen zeigen können. Diese sollen indirekt über das von Magnonenpaaren emittierte Licht gemessen werden. Damit eröffnet MIRAGE ein neues Forschungsfeld der Quantendynamik bei hohen Frequenzen und schafft die Grundlage für künftige Quanteninformationstechnologien weit über heutige Leistungsgrenzen hinaus.
An dem Projekt beteiligt sind Dr. Davide Bossine vom Fachbereich Physik der Universität Konstanz als Sprecher, Prof. Dr. Olena Gomonay, Professorin am Institut für Physik der JGU, und Prof. Hariom Jani, Professor für Quantenmaterialien an der Universität Oxford. Die CZS fördert das Projekt von März 2027 bis Februar 2029 mit 900.000 Euro. Zirka 113.000 Euro davon fließen an die JGU.
Über die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung
Die Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung fördert Wissenschaft und Lehre in den MINT-Disziplinen, Mathematik, Informatik, Naturwissenschaften und Technik. Als Partnerin exzellenter Wissenschaft ermöglicht sie Freiräume für Grundlagen- und anwendungsorientierte Forschung. Die Stiftung wurde 1889 von Ernst Abbe in Jena gegründet und ist heute eine der großen privaten wissenschaftsfördernden Stiftungen in Deutschland. Sie ist alleinige Eigentümerin der Carl Zeiss AG und der SCHOTT AG. Ihre Fördertätigkeit wird aus den Dividendenausschüttungen der beiden Stiftungsunternehmen finanziert.

title: Elements Green receives grid connection commitment from TenneT for 1.6 GWh BESS in Germany - Energy Storage
content: Another large-scale energy storage project is taking shape: Elements Green’s German subsidiary has signed a grid connection agreement with transmission system operator TenneT for a battery storage facility in Stadorf near Uelzen. The facility will have a capacity of 400 MW and a storage capacity of 1.6 GWh. It will be directly connected to the high-voltage grid. Following the signing of the connection construction contract at the beginning of this year, the grid connection contract represents another important step toward realizing the project. The next steps include detailed planning of the grid connection infrastructure and preparation for construction. Elements Green signed a deal with Envision Energy , likely for its Gen-8 battery energy storage system, for the supply of the BESS back at Intersolar 2026 in Munich. Two billion euros investment planned The London-based company is developing several more large-scale battery storage systems in Germany, intended to connect to the high-voltage grid. Elements Green is responsible for financing, developing, and operating the storage facilities. Just over a year ago, Elements Green announced its intention to connect eight battery storage systems with a combined capacity of 3.2 GW to the grid in Germany by 2027. This includes a 400 MW storage system with a four-hour storage duration in Alfstedt near Bremerhaven. At the time, the company said it planned to invest a total of two billion euros in Germany by the end of 2028. “Germany needs not only additional renewable generation capacity but, above all, the high-performance and flexible infrastructure to make the energy transition a technical and economic success. Large-scale battery storage systems such as Stadorf will play a central role in this,” Zimmermann added. title: Flower plans 2 GWh BESS in Germany, near Berlin - Energy Storage
content: Flower plans to build a 500 MW/2,000 MWh battery storage system at the Ragow substation in Lübbenau, some 100 kilometers south-east of Berlin, and near a popular tourist destination. The Swedish company acquired the project last year and is currently developing it with DCES, it announced Monday. DCES leads project development, while Flower is to handle financing, technical planning, procurement, construction and, later, operation and marketing. Building permit applications have been submitted. Flower expects the project in Brandenburg’s Spreewald region to reach ready-to-build status this year, with commercial operation scheduled for 2029. DCES has been developing projects in Germany for twelve years and holds a nationwide pipeline of 3,000 MW. The company said it will handle planning and development of the large-scale storage systems, as well as coordination with local stakeholders. Flower has only been active in the German market since last year, but it is expanding its pipeline rapidly. This year, it acquired a 112 MW battery storage portfolio from Chint Solar , plus a further 63 MW/257 MWh project in Saxony-Anhalt. It is also building self-developed projects, including a 100 MW/400 MWh system in Hamburg-Bergedorf. Beyond acquisitions, Flower has signed a virtual flexibility purchase agreement (FPA) with Engie in Germany. The virtual tolling deal secures financing for battery storage systems totaling 126 MW . Next year, Flower also plans to launch its in-house asset optimization algorithm on the German market, enabling coordinated control of energy assets. title: Cyprus: Batteries installed in summer still await grid connection - Energy Storage
content: Limassol-headquartered CYPV Solar Holdings LTD installed six batteries at six of its solar parks in July . Of these energy storage systems, only one is operational, while the remaining five batteries are still awaiting grid connection terms from the local network operator . The six installed batteries have a combined capacity of 24 MW AC/55.6 MWh, and they were installed along six photovoltaic parks totaling 24 MW, a spokesperson for CYPV Solar Holdings told ESS News . Of these hybrid projects, only one is fully operational since July . Also remarkable is that the documentation of all applications for the grid connection of the six batteries filed in 2025 was identical . There is no difference between the kind of information and documents submitted for the five projects still waiting in the queue and that of the battery project that received grid connection terms, said the CYPV Solar Holdings spokesman . The company has lodged appeals with the network operator but hasn’t received a response yet . The sole operational project comprises 1 MW of a solar system and 1 MW/5.6 MWh of a battery . Moreover, all six batteries are installed in front of the meter . “The batteries are co-located (hybrid) storage installed in front of the meter. Each battery is AC-coupled to its PV park and shares the park’s single grid connection point and export limit. There is no on-site consumption load. The battery stores the park’s own output and exports it later through the same connection. It does not add export capacity beyond the PV rating,” said CYPV Solar Holdings . Apart from CYPV Solar Holdings’s 5.6 MWh operational battery system, Cyprus had also installed a separate utility battery in the summer through the Pavlina Memorial Energy Park , a hybrid facility combining 1.8 MW of photovoltaic generation with a 5 MWh battery . Electricity supplier Petrolina Electric, who is the investor behind the ‘Pavlina Memorial Energy Park’, claimed this was Cyprus’ first utility battery system that participated in the country’s electricity market . Cyprus has so far installed a bit over 1 GW of solar PV capacity but faces an acute green energy curtailment problem . In the first five months of 2026, Cyprus curtailed over 65% of potential solar generation and the country desperately needs energy storage systems . However, the case concerning CYPV Solar Holdings’s installed batteries that await grid connection since July shows Cyprus is unable to provide timely solutions . title: Ampeak completes battery installation at 240 MWh Uskmouth project - Energy Storage
content: Scotland-headquartered developer and operator Ampeak Energy has completed the delivery and installation of all battery units and major equipment for the first phase of its 120 MW / 240 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at the Uskmouth Sustainable Energy Park in Newport, South Wales. This marks a key construction milestone, with energization planned later this month. The Afon Wysg 1 (AW1) project is scheduled to enter commercial operation in Q1 2027. Ampeak is also progressing plans to expand the site to 480 MWh, with financial close for the second phase targeted shortly after the initial project becomes operational. Ampeak said that Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage supplied 55 battery units for AW1 and will be responsible for commissioning. Jones Bros Civil Engineering UK completed installation of the batteries, along with 36 inverters, 18 twin skids, and the project’s main grid transformer. The project was given a Notice of Decision by the Newport City Council on 8th May 2025, and initial phases of the project, including a submitted “Battery Management Plan: Afon Wysg Battery Energy Storage System by Enso Energy” was first submitted in July 2023. Enso Energy sold the project to the then SAE Renewables which rebranded as Ampeak in August 2025. Now, construction works have also been completed, including concrete foundations, installation of power conversion system infrastructure and construction of a new on-site substation. Ampeak said about two-thirds of the existing power station export cable and also listed other measures to reduce overall environmental impacts, including reusing materials such as crushed concrete and an attenuation pond set up to reduce run-off. The developer said the site has been designed to accommodate future expansion, with foundations already poured and space left between the batteries for the second phase. “We’re thrilled to see the project continuing its excellent progress and look forward to reaching our next major milestone, which will be the first energization of the batteries from the grid later this month, which will be followed by the charge and discharge commissioning, all ensuring that we reach our target for energization this month and full commercial operation in Q1 2027,” said Ampeak’s CEO Designate, David Taaffe. “We will then move to rapidly financially close the expansion to 480 MWh which can be implemented with minimal disruption to the 240 MWh operating asset.” More: Canadian Solar’s e-Storage aims to supply around 1 GW of BESS capacity for Brazil’s first capacity reserve auction , scheduled for December 2 The post Ampeak completes battery installation at 240 MWh Uskmouth project appeared first on Energy Storage .

title: Australian developer seeks suppliers for 450 MW BESS and solar project - Energy Storage
content: Renewables developer Central Queensland Power (CQP) has launched an expressions of interest (EOI) process seeking suppliers for the proposed Wooderson solar and battery energy storage project being developed near the Queensland industrial hub of Gladstone. The project , planned for a site at Mount Alma, approximately 40 km southwest of Gladstone, includes a 450 MW solar facility along with a 450 MW DC-coupled battery energy storage system (BESS) with up to 3,600 MWh of storage. CQP, a joint venture between Sydney-based Energy Estate and the Australian arm of United Kingdom-headquartered clean energy company RES, has now opened an EOI through Gateway by ICN. Anticipated supply chain requirements span civil and electrical balance of plant works, equipment supply, high-voltage infrastructure, transport, logistics, commissioning and skilled labour. The developer is aiming to secure the supply of about 980,000 solar panels, a 450 MW BESS, substation, switching yard, 275 kV transmission connection, electrical infrastructure, access roads and construction facilities. Procurement for lead construction contractors is expected to progress later this year with construction currently targeted for the first quarter of 2028, with completion expected by December 2030, subject to approvals, financing and investment decisions. Small works procurement is expected to begin approximately six to nine months before construction. CQP estimates the Wooderson project will generate up to 680 jobs during the construction phase, and, once operational, would deliver about 1,300 GWh of renewable energy into the National Electricity Market a year. The project recently secured the first of three required planning approvals, covering a section of the proposed overhead transmission line within the Callide Infrastructure Corridor State Development Area (CICSDA). The project also holds an earlier environmental clearance from the Australian government, which determined it was not a controlled action under the EPBC Act. The project needs to also go through the Queensland government State Assessment and Referral Agency (SARA) for the solar farm and ancillary infrastructure including the BESS, and the Gladstone Regional Council for sections of the proposed overhead transmission line and switchyard located outside the CICSDA. title: Solar recycling 2.0 - pv magazine Global
content:
A number of companies in the United States are vying to leverage capital, experience, and new technology ahead of a wave of end-of-life solar panels expected in the coming years.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the annual volume of end-of-life crystalline silicon modules in the US is expected to hit 87,000 metric tons (MT) by 2030 and skyrocket to 820,000 MT by 2050.
With that volume comes economic opportunity. In 2023, analysts at Rystad Energy estimated the global value of recycled solar materials would hit $2.7 billion in 2030, rising to $80 billion by 2050. Assuming a 15-year panel lifespan, Rystad’s research estimated end-of-life solar modules in North America would be worth $1.4 billion in 2037 – about 15% of the global total.

Material values
Most of the material in a solar module is glass, which typically accounts for between 70% and 76% of a module’s weight. The second-largest portion is the aluminum frame, accounting for between 8% and 13%. But the most valuable material inside most solar modules is silver.
Silver now represents an important strategic asset to the United States. Along with silicon, ­silver was added to the US Critical Minerals List in November 2025.
In solar manufacturing, paste formed with the precious metal is screen printed in thin lines onto the surface of a silicon solar cell to collect and transport electrical current. It accounts for around 60% of the cost of those cells, and 10% of the total cost of a solar module.
According to the IEA, solar silver consumption was around 10 mg/W in 2024, down from 16 mg/W in 2020. While this equates to only about 0.05% of a panel’s total weight, the concentration of silver in a solar module rivals that found in many silver ores currently being mined.
That number was even higher for modules produced further in the past, meaning the coming wave of end-of-life modules will be rich in their most valuable component. The trouble is, once the cells are sealed inside layers of encapsulant, the metal contents have proven very difficult to recover without a high-temperature smelting process.
It is common practice for PV recycling companies to separate the glass and frame on the outside of a module, while the laminated components on the inside are shredded and sent to other recyclers often overseas, or even to landfill.
“The industry as a whole up to now has been on a 1.0 system, if you will,” said Adam Saghei, CEO of We Recycle Solar (WRS), in an interview with pv magazine USA. “It’s about shredding. It is heavily dependent on a mechanical process.”
When that shredded material is exported, the valuable silver, silicon, copper, and other trace metals trapped in the encapsulant are exported, too.
In addition, the recovered glass often contains impurities that make it unsuitable for use in high-temperature, closed-loop remanufacturing, such as new solar glass, instead of being used in “down-cycled” applications such as road base, concrete aggregate, and sandblasting media. All of that is changing now.
Latest technology
A number of US companies have developed alternative technologies to capture a much greater proportion of valuable solar materials and sell them domestically.
In September, WRS announced that it planned to open what it called “the nation’s first end-to-end critical materials recovery facility for retired solar panels” on a 10-acre site in Dallas, Texas, by the third quarter of 2027. The company says its “recycling 2.0” process allows it to recover up to 96% of the silver, copper, silicon, aluminum, and glass from end-of-life solar panels.
“Our approach is a little bit different,” said Saghei. “It’s on a very small footprint with regenerative solvents.” He added that the process results in glass with less than 10 parts per million of impurities. “That is essentially pure enough for you to drink out of. It’s as pure as glass comes.”
Meanwhile, OnePlanet Solar has been operating its commercial demonstration plant in Florida since early 2024. The plant is capable of processing 480,000 end-of-life solar modules in a year, equal to around 19,000 tons of material. According to the company, 100% of the outputs of this facility have been sold and consumed within the United States.
In August 2026, OnePlanet unveiled its new “PRISM” process (short for “Photovoltaic Recycling through Integrated Systems and Mechanics”). The company says PRISM results in 99% pure glass before any size reduction step, for both single side and bifacial modules, and also yields a concentrated silicon product with 95% purity that contains 1% silver.
Recycling of end-of-life modules using the PRISM process is expected to begin in 2027, and OnePlanet’s next goal is to refine its own metallurgical-grade silicon (MGS) while capturing the silver as a secondary finished product.
Another US company building out its recycling capabilities is Comstock Metals, which is now in the beginning stages of operating a solar recycling facility in Silver Springs, Nevada. The facility was first commissioned and tested in August 2026, and the company is working to ramp the plant up to 25% of its rated output capacity of 100,000 tons per year.
Comstock is also practicing a new, proprietary process at the Silver Spring site, designed to completely decompose adhesives, encapsulant, and plastic materials before the remaining components of the panel are sorted and separated for additional processing. Judd Merrill, the company’s chief financial officer, explained that the company’s current strategy is to retain the metal-rich material for its own proprietary metals recovery process.
Comstock’s plans for that metal recovery process start with a pilot-scale metals recovery operation, also planned for Silver Springs. “We are developing proprietary extraction and recovery technologies specifically designed to process the concentrated material generated by our solar recycling system. That material contains multiple valuable metals and other recoverable materials, and our objective is to recover those materials into marketable products for domestic reuse without conventional smelting,” said Merrill.
Comstock’s goal is to have a pilot-scale metal recovery line “operating continuously and reliably” by the end of 2026.
Building relationships
A key step in the success of any business is the development of ongoing relationships with partners. For solar recyclers, those relationships are made with entities on both sides of the recycling process.
On the supply side, this means contracting with manufacturers, EPCs, and re-powering companies. Comstock, for example, has minted deals with RWE for decommissioning aged solar panels as well as agreeing to take manufacturing byproducts from solar manufacturer Illuminate USA.
Similarly, leading recycler Solarcycle has partnered with Silfab, Canadian Solar, and Qcells to recycle factory defects and has inked agreements with major developers including Sunrun, EDP Renewables, AES, Orsted, and Greenbacker. The company has also announced public offtake agreements for the outputs of its recycling process. It has signed agreements with Silfab and Illuminate USA for new solar glass made from recycled modules.
Solarcycle is currently in the process of building a 1.1 million square foot glass plant next to its existing recycling facility in Cedartown, Georgia. With glass production at the facility slated to begin in 2028, the company is targeting enough glass production to support up to 6 GW of domestic panel assembly annually.
Regulation and certification
As of 2025, the NC Clean Energy Technology Center tracked 23 states with mandatory statewide decommissioning policies. Despite the widespread nature of those policies, laws in just four states (California, Maine, New Jersey, and New York) effectively prohibit the disposal of solar panels in landfills and dumps.
Outside those states, and in the absence of federal regulation, entities seeking to responsibly offload those products usually engage recyclers based on their own corporate ESG goals.
Obtaining quality and traceability certifications has become a key way recyclers set themselves apart from their competitors. Recyclers often pursue certification under ISO standards 9001 (Quality Management Systems), 14001 (Environmental Management Systems), and 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety).
In addition to obtaining those certifications, many companies seek listing under the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) National PV Recycling Program, which requires a facility audit and analysis of a company’s operations. SEIA currently lists 16 companies as partners under the program.
Recyclers seeking to go one step further obtain a certification from Sustainable Electronics Recycling International (SERI), which certifies PV recyclers under Appendix G of the third version of its Responsible Recycling (R2v3) standard. R2v3 requires annual surveillance audits by accredited certification bodies and complete chain of custody documentation for all materials. It also enforces safe handling procedures for panels, solar glass processing standards, and silicon wafer recovery protocols.
At the time of writing, SERI lists 30 facilities with active R2v3 certifications in North America, including the Comstock and OnePlanet facilities.
“Our view of certifications is pretty straightforward,” Connor Hogan, CFO of OnePlanet, told pv magazine USA. “If you can get a certification, you should just get a certification rather than say that you can attest to it.”
Other companies aren’t as keen on R2v3. “One issue with R2 certification is that it’s kind of open source, and when you spend years cultivating a relationship with a downstream partner, you don’t want to just give that up so everyone knows who you’re selling material to,” said Saghei, adding that “certifications are like a driver’s license – just because everyone has one doesn’t mean they’re a good driver.”
In the coming years, solar recyclers will find many ways to differentiate themselves based on the effectiveness and economics of their logistics and recovery processes, as well as the adaptability of those processes and how quickly they can scale operations.
The relationships recyclers build with manufacturers, developers, downstream offtakers, and policymakers will also be essential. They will face questions from those stakeholders about their certifications and material tracing practices and will likely be presented with new challenges as state governments take action to ensure solar module waste is recycled properly.

title: Global solar installations face first annual decline in eight years - pv magazine Global
content:
London-based analytics firm GlobalData said annual global solar PV additions will decline in 2026 for the first time since 2018, after rising 17.5% to a record in 2025. It attributed the slowdown to market reforms in China, policy changes in the United States and a slowdown in Pakistan.
“The 2026 dip reflects policy shifts in a few large markets rather than a weakening of solar’s fundamentals, with China’s move to market-based tariffs accounting for most of the decline,” said Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, a power analyst at GlobalData.
The company said it expects global cumulative PV capacity to grow at a compound annual rate of 12.5% from 2025 to 2035, more than doubling solar’s share of global electricity.
China accounted for more than half of 2025 additions, followed by the United States and India. India’s additions rose 87.2%, and Pakistan’s grew 34.3% as rooftop and off-grid demand made it the fourth-largest market. Additions in the Middle East and Africa nearly tripled, while Europe’s rose 2.6% and North America’s fell 3.6%, said GlobalData.
The company said the long decline in module prices has stalled, as higher silver and cell costs, China’s export tax rebate adjustment in April and Beijing’s “anti-involution” campaign pushed prices up in early 2026. Saibasan said grid constraints are now the main barrier to growth, pointing to curtailment in China, negative power prices in Europe and connection queues in the United States, India and Brazil.
“Falling battery costs are the main counterweight to grid congestion, curtailment, and negative power prices. Solar-plus-storage is now competitive for firm supply in high-resource regions, allowing solar to move beyond daytime generation and compete for round-the-clock supply,” he said. “Developers and investors that pair solar with storage and secure grid access early will be best placed to capture the recovery from 2027.”
The forecast follows GlobalData’s March projection that
global solar capacity will reach 6 TW by 2031
. The International Energy Agency’s Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme has estimated that
global solar additions hit 690 GW in 2025
, and in October the International Energy Agency forecast an 11% fall in global renewable capacity additions in 2026, mainly because of slower solar deployment in China.

title: Silver prices find $50 floor as solar industry seeks to accelerate shift toward copper - pv magazine Global
content:
Silver prices appear to have stabilized around $50 per ounce following an exceptionally volatile year, but the photovoltaic industry should not expect a return to the much lower prices of previous decades, according to Philip Newman, managing director of
Metals Focus
“I think the price, the floor seems quite strong, but I think you’re still going to see more volatility,” Newman told
pv magazine
. “Could prices dip below 50? Of course they can. But I think the 50 still seems like a decent floor.”
His comments follow the publication of new silver market estimates by the Silver Institute and Metals Focus on November 13. The organizations expect the global silver market to record its sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with demand exceeding supply by 35 million ounces.
Silver reached an
all-time high of $121.65 per ounce on January 26
, driven by strong investment demand and tight physical liquidity in London. It subsequently retreated to approximately $52 by November 4, as shifting US interest rate expectations, a stronger dollar and rising bond yields weighed on precious metals.
Despite the correction, prices remain exceptionally high. The annual average was approximately $40 in 2025, while Newman suggested the 2026 average could exceed $70 per ounce.
Thrifting
The impact of elevated prices is particularly apparent in photovoltaics, where manufacturers are accelerating efforts to reduce silver consumption.
According to
Metals Focus
, global industrial silver demand is expected to decline by 3% to 640 million ounces in 2026. Industrial consumption outside photovoltaics is forecast to grow by 4.5% to 492 million ounces, but this will be more than offset by weaker demand from solar cells.
The consultancy attributes the decline to slower-than-expected PV installations, particularly in China, and accelerated silver thrifting and substitution.
Newman said the industry’s response to higher prices has evolved significantly over the past year. When silver first exceeded $50 in late 2025, manufacturers focused on extending silver-coated copper metallization, already used in heterojunction (HJT) cells, to tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) technology.
Replacing silver entirely with copper was still regarded as a longer-term objective because of potential performance trade-offs. However, January’s price surge changed the discussion.
“Let’s move to copper and we can think about the trade-off afterwards and improve the efficiency,” Newman said, describing the industry’s initial reaction.
Since then, the transition has become more measured, with manufacturers considering not only conversion efficiency but also long-term reliability.
“I think the move to copper has now become more measured,” Newman said, pointing to growing attention to “the shelf life, the longevity of these cells.”
Manufacturers and buyers have different priorities
According to Newman, the transition is also shaped by diverging interests among manufacturers and module buyers.
For manufacturers facing overcapacity and intense price competition, reducing silver consumption represents an opportunity to lower costs. Developers and installers, however, may hesitate to adopt new metallization technologies without sufficient evidence of long-term reliability.
“From the panel manufacturer, to your point about overcapacity and the pressure on costs, they would really like to move to copper quite quickly,” Newman said. “On the other side, the companies that are buying those panels and installing them, I think there’s a lot more hesitancy, more reticence, more cautiousness about doing so.”
This divergence could encourage manufacturers to offer conventional high-silver modules alongside alternatives with reduced silver content or potentially silver-free metallization.
Although research into copper metallization has intensified, fully copper-based solutions have yet to become mainstream in commercial TOPCon products. Intermediate approaches involving silver-coated copper or lower silver loadings appear more realistic in the near term.
The economic incentive remains substantial even after the recent price correction.
Newman estimated that at $60 per ounce, silver accounts for approximately 17% of TOPCon module costs. At $50, the proportion falls to around 14%, compared with roughly 11% when silver traded at $40.
Metals Focus
expects global PV installations to decline modestly in 2026 before returning to growth in 2027. Nevertheless, Newman expects silver thrifting to continue, even if prices stabilize.
Silver shortages unlikely
Despite the sixth consecutive annual market deficit, Newman does not anticipate a physical shortage that would materially disrupt photovoltaic manufacturing.
“No, not really,” he said when asked about potential supply problems.
He pointed to China’s substantial silver imports in 2026, continued availability of silver powder from Japan, and gradually recovering inventories in London.
The Silver Institute expects total silver supply to decline by 3% to approximately 1.045 billion ounces in 2026. Mine production should remain broadly stable at 834 million ounces, while recycling is forecast to increase by 6% to 210 million ounces.
The overall deficit is expected to narrow from 54 million ounces in 2025 to 35 million ounces in 2026, bringing the cumulative shortfall since 2021 to approximately 746 million ounces.
Newman acknowledged that sudden increases in investment demand could generate temporary physical market tightness.
“I don’t think you would ever say never, but I think it’s unlikely,” he said when asked about a repetition of the severe market tightness experienced in October 2025.
He added that metal could be transported from CME inventories to London to relieve pressure, even if renewed investment demand temporarily pushed silver lease rates higher.
The role of interest rates
Looking beyond photovoltaics, Newman believes monetary policy and investor expectations will remain major influences on silver prices.
Geopolitical tensions can support precious metals through safe-haven demand, but rising energy prices can also reinforce inflation concerns and expectations of higher US interest rates.
“I think you’re going to look at each on a case-by-case basis,” Newman said, referring to the impact of geopolitical crises such as the war in Iran.
Silver’s outlook also remains closely linked to gold, which Newman expects to face continued pressure until Federal Reserve policy becomes clearer.
“I think gold will remain under pressure until we have clarity from the Fed,” he said, although he believes the $4,000-per-ounce level could hold.
Metals Focus
‘ central scenario assumes tensions surrounding Iran will gradually de-escalate sufficiently to ease inflation expectations and limit further US interest rate increases. Under those conditions, investment demand for precious metals could strengthen again in 2027.
“Maybe it doesn’t happen that early next year. But maybe by the summer, prices for gold and silver are considerably higher than we see today,” Newman said.
For the photovoltaic industry, such a scenario would reinforce the case for reducing silver consumption, even if the recent price correction has eased immediate cost pressures. The central challenge remains balancing the savings offered by copper-based metallization against the efficiency and long-term reliability requirements of commercial solar modules.

title: Why silicon won the solar race and what emerging PV technologies can learn from thin film - pv magazine Global
content:
Crystalline silicon has dominated the global photovoltaic market for decades, while alternative technologies, including thin-film solar cells, have struggled to secure a comparable market share. This dominance is often attributed to technological performance, cost competitiveness and efficiency improvements. However, research from City St George’s, University of London, challenges this explanation, suggesting that the commercial success of solar technologies depends on more than their technical characteristics.
The study, “
Technology (Non)Emergence: How System Interdependencies Among Activities by Heterogeneous Actors Shaped Alternative Solar Technology Trajectories
,” published in
Organization Science
, examines how manufacturing capabilities, accumulated industrial knowledge, investment patterns and policy support influence competition between PV technologies.
“We can think of competition as competition between manufacturing ecosystems, rather than competition in terms of technological characteristics such as efficiency, cost or other design elements,” lead researcher Mara Guerra told
pv magazine
. “This does not mean that technological characteristics are not important, but that competition depends on how manufacturing ecosystems evolve with respect to market requirements.”
According to Guerra, even technologies with promising performance characteristics may struggle commercially without the manufacturing infrastructure, industrial expertise and market support needed to scale production.
“Not even the best-performing tech can succeed if the system of activities around it fails to support its interface with evolving requirements of the market,” she said.
Thin film’s missed opportunity
The researchers found that thin-film PV technologies could have achieved greater commercial success if industrial investments and policy interventions had followed a different path.
“Hindsight is amazing, but thin film could have had greater success with a different pattern of investment across the ecosystem,” Guerra said.
She explained that thin-film technologies struggled to compete in mainstream PV markets, which benefited from policy support and increasingly established manufacturing capabilities. At the same time, some of their characteristics made them suitable for emerging applications, such as building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV), which received comparatively limited policy attention.
“Its characteristics made it ideal for niches such as building-integrated PV which did not receive as much support. Bold policy interventions in these more transformative markets may have helped thin film achieve a larger market share,” Guerra said.
The study also identified shortcomings in investment strategies across the thin-film industry. Rather than prioritizing shared manufacturing knowledge, compatibility with existing industrial processes or expertise from related sectors, investments often focused on the technological uniqueness of individual approaches.
While this differentiation helped attract investors, it did not necessarily support manufacturing scalability.
“Higher investments that rewarded reusing existing manufacturing knowledge or focusing on manufacturing compatibilities could have contributed to more rapid scaling of the technology and larger market share in the mainstream markets,” Guerra said.
The findings suggest that commercial success depends not only on technological breakthroughs, but also on the ability to develop manufacturing processes and industrial knowledge that can be replicated and deployed at scale.
Lessons for perovskites and tandem
The researchers said the historical development of thin-film PV offers important lessons for emerging technologies, including perovskite solar cells and silicon-perovskite tandems, which are attracting significant investment but still face commercialization challenges.
According to Guerra, developers should focus on two priorities: demonstrating reproducible technological performance and balancing innovation with manufacturing standardization.
“Firstly, entrants must move beyond technological records to achieve credible and replicable performance earlier on,” she said. “Technological breakthroughs are useful to build expectations, but in the end commercialization requires demonstrating that these breakthroughs can be consistently reproduced.”
Laboratory efficiency records can generate investor interest and strengthen expectations surrounding emerging PV technologies. However, they may also introduce uncertainty if the reported performance cannot be consistently reproduced.
“Performance records attract investment and generate enthusiasm but may also create unrealistic expectations. When performance records cannot be verified or replicated, they can create more uncertainty than they resolve,” Guerra said.
The second lesson concerns the relationship between technological differentiation and industrial standardization. According to the researcher, thin-film manufacturers frequently emphasized proprietary technological approaches and distinct manufacturing ecosystems, limiting opportunities to benefit from established industrial knowledge and common production practices.
“Thin film overemphasized uniqueness across technology and ecosystems. This helped with attracting investment but undermined scalability,” Guerra said. “Those who combined innovation and uniqueness in their technology with standardization in manufacturing or leveraging existing knowledge from related industries did better when commercializing their technology.”
Can industrial policy reshape PV competition?
The findings also have implications for governments seeking to develop domestic PV manufacturing capabilities and compete with established production ecosystems.
According to Guerra, mature industrial ecosystems benefit from accumulated manufacturing expertise, supplier networks and industrial knowledge that reinforce their competitive advantages. Although these advantages become increasingly difficult to challenge over time, they do not necessarily prevent new manufacturing ecosystems from emerging.
“While challenging an established advantage is increasingly difficult, especially when it is based on existing manufacturing ecosystems that have accumulated capabilities and knowledge that positively reinforce each other, this does not obstruct the creation of new successful and competitive manufacturing ecosystems,” she said.
Guerra argued that the effectiveness of public support depends on how emerging industrial ecosystems position themselves relative to established competitors.
Rather than attempting to replicate existing manufacturing structures or directly displace dominant producers, policymakers could support complementary technologies, specialized manufacturing activities and new market segments.
“The effectiveness of public support in creating competitive manufacturing ecosystems depends on how new ecosystems position themselves relative to others,” Guerra said. “Rather than trying to replicate or dislodge an existing ecosystem, focusing on support or complementary technologies and activities can contribute to the creation of a new and localized industrial advantage.”

title: Coal plant failure, not solar PV, triggered Sri Lanka’s latest blackout - pv magazine Global
content:
The cause of
Sri Lanka’s nationwide black occurred on Oct. 17
was the the loss of 187 MW of electricity from a coal power plant and not the high solar PV penetration as initially thought.
This emerges from a
preliminary investigation report
submitted by the National System Operator (NSO) to the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL), which explicitly identifies the sudden loss of generation from Lakvijaya Coal Power Plant Unit 1 (LVPP Unit 01) as the initiating event of the blackout.
“LVPP Unit 01 rapidly de-loaded from the unit net generation of 187 MW to 5 MW within 450 ms,” the authors of the report state, noting that grid frequency fell from 49.906 Hz to 48.75 Hz within two seconds.
The unit has a capacity of 300 MW and is located at the 900 MW Norochcholai Power Station in Puttalam, in the country’s North Western Province.
The report does not fully explain why the coal unit lost output or whether distributed PV behaviour contributed to the cascading failure.
Following the blackout, the NSO instructed all PV system owners to disconnect their installations from the grid. The decision appeared to have been informed by a previous nationwide blackout on Feb. 9, 2025, when the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) identified high solar PV penetration as a major contributing factor.
According to a CEB investigation published in April 2025, the blackout was triggered at noon by a fault at the Panadura grid substation. At the time, solar PV accounted for more than 50% of electricity demand, leaving the grid with insufficient system inertia to withstand the disturbance. The resulting voltage drop and cascading disconnections led to a nationwide blackout.
At the time, the authorities also instructed rooftop solar system owners to disconnect their installations from the grid during restoration efforts.
Sri Lanka’s rooftop PV capacity reached
1.94 GW by the end of 2025
, following rapid growth in installations and generation.
Sri Lanka’s daily electricity demand stood at approximately 58 GWh to 60 GWh in March 2026, equivalent to an average continuous power requirement of around 2,400 MW to 2,500 MW.

content:
The Korea Energy Agency (KEA) said last week that it has launched its 2026 Community Solar program. The initiative supports energy storage systems run by VPP operators in grid-saturated areas.
The KEA said the program is intended to help establish “sunlight income villages” in parts of the network that have little spare capacity left for new generation. Under the government’s sunlight income village policy, residents take part in local renewable energy projects, and the generation revenue goes to village welfare and community activities.
The call for proposals runs from Nov. 13 to Dec. 11. The KEA said it will accept applications by email from 9 a.m. on Nov. 16 until 6 p.m. on Dec. 11 (KST). The online notice does not state the program’s budget, subsidy rate or project size limits. The agency has attached the program’s operating rules to the notice, along with a document on the status of distribution lines by region in areas linked to the solar villages.
South Korea
selected 86 communities for the scheme
community solar cooperative push
, with financial support covering up to 85% of solar installation costs.
The storage subsidies add to South Korea’s grid-scale procurement. In September, the government

title: Japan sees increase in corporate solar PPAs - pv magazine Global
content:
The number of corporate solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) signed in Japan is increasing, according to analysis from infrastructure intelligence platform Global Infrastructure Sherpa.
Roberto Krell, founder of Global Infrastructure Sherpa, told
pv magazine
the company logged around 30% more corporate solar PPAs in Japan from January to October this year than across the first ten months of 2025.
Notable examples of agreements signed this year include two solar PPAs between Microsoft and pan-Asian renewable energy platform Blueleaf Energy, announced late last month, with Microsoft acting as the sole offtaker for two solar projects due online mid next year. In May, Spanish developer EDP Renewables commissioned a 44 MW solar project in Fukushima for Amazon under a long-term corporate PPA.
Global Infrastructure Sherpa says that while large-scale players, such as Microsoft and Amazon continue to attract attention, Japan’s corporate PPA market is moving beyond the hyperscalers with manufacturers, logistics companies and advertising groups also entering into long-term solar agreements.
Examples include a 15-year virtual PPA involving a 54 MW solar plant and approximately 130 MWh of battery storage between Japanese manufacturer NSK and Tokyo-based developer Eneos Renewable Energy and a 20-year solar PPA in Hyogo and Kyoto between Nippon Electric Glass and Japanese utility Kansai Electric that is expected to begin delivery in March next year.
Krell told
pv magazine
climate targets are driving corporate solar PPAs in Japan, with some companies looking to solar deals to meet carbon-neutrality targets.
He cited virtual PPAs as another factor, noting that many of this year’s corporate solar PPAs are virtual. “The company buys the green certificates from a new solar plant at a fixed price and keeps its existing electricity supplier,” Krell explained. “That makes a deal much easier to sign, and it’s bringing in buyers that wouldn’t have signed a few years ago, such as railways, retailers and mid-sized manufacturers.”
Krell looked to data centres as another driver. “Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Equinix and At Tokyo have all signed solar PPAs in Japan, and theirs tend to be the large ones,” he said. “[Data center company] Equinix’s 121 MW deal in February is the biggest corporate solar PPA we’ve seen in Japan this year, followed by
Tokyu Railway’s 98 MW
Krell predicted that the upward trend in corporate solar PPAs in Japan is likely to continue in the coming years.
“The data centre build-out around Tokyo and Osaka hasn’t peaked yet, and every new campus is another potential buyer. More companies also have climate targets to meet, and virtual PPAs make it easy for them to sign,” he told
pv magazine
.  “What could slow things down may be challenges like finding good sites without local opposition, and getting grid connections in time.”
Analysis published last year by data platform Japanese Energy Hub said that, since the first corporate PPA in Japan was signed in 2021, the number of disclosed deals has grown to over 500, totaling over 2.5 GW in installed and planned capacity.
Japan’s cumulative solar capacity is estimated at around 100 GW after adding approximately
5.8 GW of solar
last year.

content:
The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) is advising households with solar installations to check if their current energy contract is still the most suitable ahead of the
end of net-metering
on Jan. 1, 2027.
The end of net metering will mean households can no longer offset electricity exported to the grid against electricity imported from it. ACM’s latest update explains that from the start of next year, households will pay the full retail electricity rate, including energy taxes, for power drawn from the grid, while receiving a separate feed-in payment for surplus electricity.
The regulator adds that the feed-in payment is generally lower than the retail electricity rate. Under Dutch legislation, suppliers must pay at least 50% of the basic electricity supply rate, excluding taxes, for exported electricity until Dec. 31, 2029.
ACM is expecting feed-in charges to decline after the scheme ends, as suppliers will no longer incur costs associated with net metering, but adds that suppliers will continue to face other costs related to solar customers, including expenses associated with balancing the electricity grid when solar generation fluctuates unexpectedly.
ACM, which is responsible for supervising the tariffs of energy suppliers, says it will now include contracts with feed-in charges for solar panels in its monthly overview, known as Energiemonitor. Its most recent monitor says a number of suppliers are charging significantly higher rates for their standard contracts as opposed to dynamic contracts.
The discontinuation of net metering may make home batteries more attractive for some households, ACM added.
The number of home batteries is
growing significantly
in the Netherlands. Figures from ACM state approximately 89,000 home batteries belonging to households and small businesses were registered with grid operators by the end of October but add that as small plug-in battery systems are not always registered, the total is likely even higher. Total installed home battery capacity amounted to 1.1 GW by the end of October, compared to 0.3 GW at the end of October 2025.
ACM says consumers considering a home battery should carefully check what best suits their individual situation.
“Whether a home battery is worthwhile depends, among other things, on the home, energy consumption, and the energy contract,” the regulator said. “Before purchasing a home battery, it is therefore wise to first determine how much energy you use, where you can save, and what suits your home.”
It also warned against unreliable sellers taking advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the end of the net metering scheme.
“They are luring consumers into expensive purchases with misleading sales pitches, sometimes home batteries costing more than €20,000 [$22,035],” ACM said.
ACM’s latest update also reveals that negative electricity prices in the Netherlands currently stand at just over 400 in 2026, lower than in the same period of 2025 and 2024. The regulator says a possible explanation for this is the increase in the number of installed batteries.

title: Mitsubishi Electric unveils ‘The Little One’ heat pump - pv magazine Global
content:
Japanese electronics and electrical equipment manufacturing company
Mitsubishi Electric
has unveiled a new residential air-to-water heat pump designed for new-build homes in the United Kingdom.
The new system, called The Little One, is part of the manufacturer’s
Ecodan product range
and will be commercially available in 2027.
The company said it developed the unit to address space constraints, installation flexibility and costs for housebuilders preparing for the UK’s Future Homes Standard, which is a building regulation framework designed to ensure new homes are highly energy-efficient and produce significantly lower carbon emissions, primarily through low-carbon heating and improved insulation.
The heat pump uses propane (R290) as its refrigerant and is available in two versions with heating capacities of 4 kW and 6 kW. Both models have an A+++ energy efficiency rating.
The 4 kW model achieves a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) of 4.77 at a water flow temperature of 35 C, while the 6 kW version reaches 4.65 under the same conditions, according to the manufacturer.
The unit measures 970 mm × 713 mm × 400 mm and weighs 58 kg. According to Mitsubishi Electric, it is 47% smaller and 40% lighter than a comparable model in its existing product range.
The system incorporates the company’s patented Bossless Fan technology, which is designed to reduce weight and operating noise by eliminating the conventional central fan hub. The 4 kW model has a sound power level of 49 dB(A), compared with 51 dB(A) for the 6 kW version.
Mitsubishi Electric said the heat pump also features patented refrigerant technology that incorporates an odorant into the R290 circuit. According to the manufacturer, this eliminates the need for a protective zone around the outdoor unit, allowing greater flexibility in installation locations.
The company said the new range is designed to be more cost-effective than its existing R32 and R290 heat pump offerings, although it did not disclose pricing information.
“By making the unit considerably smaller and lighter, reducing noise, removing the need for an R290 protective zone and delivering excellent efficiency at a more competitive cost, we believe we have created a product that makes specifying and installing heat pumps easier for housebuilders,” said Joanna Crown, product marketing manager at Mitsubishi Electric.
No further technical details about the heat pump technology have been disclosed.
